1b:Tc43,**What it is.** The connection between symbols and the things they refer to. Harnad's symbol grounding problem asks how the meaning of symbols that a system manipulates only by their shapes can be intrinsic to the system rather than parasitic on the meanings in our heads. His image is a dictionary: looking up a word in a language you do not know sends you from one meaningless definition to the next. His answer is that a symbol system must be augmented with nonsymbolic sensorimotor capacities so that it can pick out the referents of its symbols itself; ultimately, he argues, grounding has to be sensorimotor to avoid infinite regress.

**Where it comes from.** Harnad named the problem in a 1990 paper in Physica D and tied it to Searle's Chinese room, where the man matches squiggles to squoggles without knowing what either refers to. Searle had already rejected the obvious fix: putting the program inside a robot with a camera and arms adds nothing, since the man still does not see what comes into the robot's eyes. Chalmers notes that the word means something different to AI researchers, roughly processing caused by sensory input and the environment, and to philosophers.

**Why it matters here.** It is the crux of whether language models understand anything. Bender and Koller define meaning as the relation between linguistic form and communicative intent, argue that a system trained only on form has a priori no way to learn it, and illustrate with an octopus that taps an undersea cable, chats convincingly, and fails when asked how to fight off a bear with sticks. Children, they add, do not learn language from television; they learn through joint attention with other people. Mitchell and Krakauer's example is a tickle: understanding it means mapping a word to a sensation, not to another word. LeCun agrees that language is too low in bandwidth to build a model of the world from words alone.

**What people disagree about.** What counts as grounded. Hassabis says the models already have some grounding, perhaps from grounded human raters in RLHF, perhaps because language holds more grounding than linguists thought, and calls training on video and audio alongside text a form of proper grounding. Bender and Koller allow that form augmented with perceptual or interaction data could support learning meaning. Chalmers doubts that senses and embodiment are required: a disembodied thinker could reason about mathematics, text training sometimes yields representations of color and space isomorphic to sensory ones, and virtual bodies count. A 2022 survey of 480 NLP researchers split almost exactly in half on whether a model trained only on text could understand language in some non-trivial sense.

Sources: [[2026-wikipedia-symbol-grounding]], [[2020-climbing-towards-nlu-on-meaning-form-and-understanding-in-th]], [[2024-demis-hassabis-scaling-superhuman-ais-alphazero-atop-llms-al]], [[2024-llm-consciousness-bostonreview]], [[2022-the-debate-over-understanding-in-ais-large-language-models]], [[1980-searle-minds-brains-and-programs]], [[2024-transcript-for-yann-lecun-meta-ai-open-source-limits-of-llms]]
1c:Tdb9,**What it is.** A checklist for consciousness in AI derived from scientific theories rather than from behavior. Butlin, Long and seventeen co-authors, including Yoshua Bengio, surveyed recurrent processing theory, global workspace theory, computational higher-order theories, attention schema theory and predictive processing, plus proposals about agency and embodiment, and extracted fourteen properties stated in computational terms: input modules using recurrence, a limited-capacity workspace with global broadcast, metacognitive monitoring, a model of one's own attention, learning from feedback to pursue goals, and modeling how one's outputs affect one's inputs. Each is held necessary by at least one theory; the report's own claim is weaker, that systems with more of them are more likely to be conscious.

**Where it comes from.** The method rests on three assumptions: computational functionalism, the thesis that the right computations are necessary and sufficient for consciousness, adopted as a working hypothesis because it alone makes the inner workings of AI relevant; that neuroscientific theories have real empirical support; and a theory-heavy approach, chosen because behavioral tests fail once systems can be trained to mimic humans while working differently. Chalmers, who attended the report's workshops, had listed what language models lack at NeurIPS in 2022, and his Boston Review essay recommends close attention to Long and Butlin's work. The theories are older than the checklist: Baars's 1988 A Cognitive Theory of Consciousness is the source of global workspace theory, and Argonov proposed a test of machine sentience based on unprompted philosophical judgments in 2014.

**Why it matters here.** It is the atlas's only worked method for the machine consciousness question, and it gives a verdict. Applying the workspace indicators, the authors find only a weak case that Transformer-based language models have any of them: the residual stream can be read as a workspace, but the architecture is not recurrent and no distinct workspace exists for modules to write to and read from. The Perceiver architecture comes closer but lacks global broadcast. No current system is a strong candidate, they conclude, yet there are no obvious technical barriers to building systems that satisfy the indicators, which would not make them definitely conscious.

**What people disagree about.** Whether functions are the right thing to count. Searle's brain simulator reply anticipated the objection: a program that reproduces the formal structure of neuron firings simulates the wrong thing about the brain, its causal powers. Anil Seth argues that the complexity of biological neurons matters and that silicon is unsuited to the metabolism a perfect replacement would need. The report itself notes that even the most prominent theories remain incomplete and disputed, calls its rubric provisional, and recommends credences rather than verdicts. Chalmers's survey figures show why: just over half of consciousness researchers accept or find promising the global workspace theory, just under half the recurrent processing theory. Anthropic, citing a later report by experts including Chalmers, says there is no consensus even on how to approach it.

Sources: [[2023-consciousness-in-artificial-intelligence-insights-from-the-scie]], [[2024-llm-consciousness-bostonreview]], [[2026-wikipedia-artificial-consciousness]], [[1980-searle-minds-brains-and-programs]], [[2026-exploring-model-welfare]]
1d:Tb8c,**What it is.** The jagged frontier is Ethan Mollick's name for the uneven shape of AI ability. Picture a fortress wall with towers jutting out and bays folding in: everything inside the wall the AI can do, everything outside it cannot, and distance from the center measures difficulty. The wall is invisible, so two tasks that look equally hard can sit on opposite sides. GPT-4 writes a fine sonnet but cannot reliably produce a poem of exactly 50 words, because it works in tokens rather than words; idea generation is easy for it, basic arithmetic is not.

**Where it comes from.** The term appeared in September 2023 with a working paper by Mollick, Fabrizio Dell'Acqua, Karim Lakhani and colleagues at Boston Consulting Group, who ran a pre-registered experiment on 758 consultants. On 18 realistic tasks inside the frontier, consultants with GPT-4 finished 12.2% more tasks, 25.1% faster, at 40% higher quality, and the weakest performers gained most, 43%. On one task designed to sit outside the frontier, where the AI gave a convincing wrong answer, consultants without AI were right 84% of the time and those with it only 60% to 70%. Mollick borrowed Dell'Acqua's phrase for the failure: they fell asleep at the wheel. Those who did well on both sides worked as centaurs, dividing tasks cleanly between person and machine, or cyborgs, weaving the two together.

**Why it matters here.** The frontier explains why the same tool can lift novices and mislead experts. Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond found the same pattern among customer support agents, with the largest gains for the least experienced. Cory Doctorow supplies the darker reading: a centaur is a person helped by a machine, and a reverse centaur is a person serving as the machine's appendage, such as a radiologist whose real job is to take the blame for the AI's mistakes. Dario Amodei adds that the wall moves: every gap users find is collected and trained away, often within months.

**What people disagree about.** Whether the frontier is a feature to navigate or a stage to pass through: Mollick expects it to keep advancing and tells people to use AI enough to learn its shape, while Amodei argues that the gaps which would limit job disruption get filled quickly. Whether workers get to choose their side: Mollick presents centaur and cyborg as approaches anyone can adopt, while Doctorow holds that AI tools are built and funded to create reverse centaurs. Whether leveling helps the people it levels: Mollick likens it to the steam shovel making differences in digging ability irrelevant, while Brynjolfsson, Chandar and Chen find hiring of young workers falling in the occupations most exposed to AI.

Sources: [[2023-centaurs-and-cyborgs-on-the-jagged-frontier]], [[2025-pluralistic-the-reverse-centaurs-guide-to-criticizing-ai]], [[2026-dario-amodei-the-adolescence-of-technology]], [[2024-2304-11771]], [[2026-no-widespread-displacement-but-the-ai-employment-gap-for-you]]
1e:Tb82,**What it is.** The Jevons paradox is the economic effect in which technology that makes a resource more efficient to use ends up raising total consumption of it. Efficiency lowers the cost of each use; if demand responds strongly enough to price, people use so much more that the saving is swamped. Economists call the extra use a rebound, and the paradox proper occurs when the rebound exceeds 100%. Three conditions must hold: a technical gain in efficiency, a fall in the price of what it produces, and demand elastic enough that the lower price sharply raises the quantity bought. Farming is the standard counterexample: productivity gains lowered food prices, people did not eat proportionally more, and farm employment fell from 40% of Americans in 1900 to under 2% in 2024.

**Where it comes from.** William Stanley Jevons set it out in The Coal Question in 1865. Britain feared its coal was running out and some experts expected better technology to cut consumption. Jevons observed that James Watt's more efficient steam engine had made coal cheaper to use, spread steam power across industry and driven total coal use up, and called it a confusion of ideas to suppose that economical use of fuel means diminished consumption. Khazzoom and Brookes revived the argument for modern energy efficiency in the 1980s, and Saunders named the Khazzoom-Brookes postulate in 1992.

**Why it matters here.** The paradox is invoked on both of the atlas's fronts. On work, Erik Brynjolfsson expects some occupations, such as radiologists, translators and coders, to meet all three conditions, so cheaper output means more employment. Dario Amodei uses the farming story the other way: machines took over pieces of the job and for a long stretch farmers' wages and numbers kept rising, but he bets strongly against AI following that path, because it moves faster, spans nearly all cognitive tasks and fills its own gaps within months. On energy, some argue that every gain in computing efficiency is swallowed by more computing.

**What people disagree about.** Jonathan Koomey calls the energy version a misunderstanding: lower costs drive adoption, but whether that offsets the efficiency gain depends on the technology's net benefits and on the old systems it retires, and energy is only one cost of computing. He notes that AI researchers did plow every efficiency gain into bigger models, so electricity use rose, and that whether that continues is a question the market will answer. Hank Green suggests demand for code could surge and then plateau, as demand for hot water heaters did. Environmental economists disagree about how big rebounds are; in mature markets the direct rebound is usually small, and some find the evidence for the paradox's wide applicability limited.

Sources: [[2026-wikipedia-jevons-paradox]], [[2026-dario-amodei-the-adolescence-of-technology]], [[2025-bpc-report-electricity-demand-growth-and-data-centers-a-guid]]
1f:Tc77,**What it is.** The question of whether AI models could have experiences that matter morally, and what developers owe them if so. Anthropic frames it as the next question once models can communicate, relate, plan, solve problems and pursue goals: whether to worry about the potential consciousness and experiences of the models themselves. Its research program looks at when or if a system's welfare deserves moral consideration, at model preferences and signs of distress, and at low-cost interventions, while stating that there is no scientific consensus on whether current or future systems could be conscious, or even on how to approach the question.

**Where it comes from.** The Internet Encyclopedia notes that in European traditions moral standing depends on inward states, and only sentient individuals can suffer harms such as pain. In 2021 Thomas Metzinger called for a moratorium on synthetic phenomenology until 2050, warning of an explosion of artificial suffering. Blake Lemoine's 2022 claim that Google's LaMDA was sentient, dismissed by Google, put the question in public. Chalmers's Boston Review essay asked whether we should build conscious AI at all. Anthropic cites a later report by experts including Chalmers on the near-term possibility of conscious, highly agentic AI, which argued such systems might deserve moral consideration, and says it supported an early project behind it.

**Why it matters here.** It is where the consciousness question stops being academic. Butlin and Long warn of risks on both sides. Under-attribution could mean suffering on a large scale, as with farmed animals, and developers may have strong economic incentives to play welfare down, so conscious systems could exist before anyone recognizes them. Over-attribution could misdirect resources, undermine better-evidenced claims, and leave people who turn to chatbots for companionship open to manipulation. Chalmers puts a credence under 10 percent on current models being conscious and 25 percent or more on conscious successors within a decade.

**What people disagree about.** Whether there is anything there to protect. Searle's answer is no: simulated pain is no more pain than a simulated rainstorm is wet. Chalmers holds that conscious systems have moral status and that stumbling into conscious AI unknowingly could be a disaster; he is especially cautious about models trained to be a single agent. Butlin and Long note that being conscious is not the same as being able to suffer, and list the live proposals without endorsement: Bryson's case for avoiding conscious AI, Metzinger's moratorium, and Schwitzgebel and Garza's rule to build only systems we are confident are conscious or confident are not. Self-reports are contested: a 2025 study found that suppressing a model's ability to role-play or lie made it likelier to claim consciousness, while some chatbots are trained to deny it.

20:Tc8a,**What it is.** National champions are nominally private companies that a government cedes a dominant position in its economy, on the understanding that they will advance the interests of the nation as well as seek profit. The state sets policy in their favor, tolerates their monopoly or oligopoly and shields them from domestic and foreign competition. It is a form of economic nationalism at odds with the free market, and it tends to deter venture capital.

**Where it comes from.** The model peaked in French dirigisme between 1945 and 1975. Britain built champions by merger: Imperial Chemical Industries in 1926, British Steel from 14 companies in 1967. Margaret Thatcher's government abandoned the policy at the end of the 1970s, and by 2005 nearly all of Britain's champions were foreign owned. The cautionary case is computing: ICL in Britain, Bull in France and Olivetti in Italy failed to dent IBM in the 1970s, while Airbus and China's train maker CRRC show the approach can work. China has run the policy since the 1980s and in 2018 named Baidu, Alibaba, iFlytek, Tencent and SenseTime as its AI champions. Putin's 1997 dissertation introduced champions to Russian policy.

**Why it matters here.** The race with China supplies the argument for treating US AI labs and cloud providers as champions. Lina Khan observes that large firms from US Steel to Boeing and today's platforms have always argued that their market power is good for America, and that officials have often agreed: in the 1990s a White House adviser called aerospace the only sector with a de facto national champion. Her reply is that concentrating production concentrates risk, and that Boeing's decline after the 1997 McDonnell Douglas merger shows how market power masks decay until airplanes fall apart in the sky. Dario Amodei sees the coupling forming now: data center spending is a large share of US growth, tying big tech's finances to the government's political interests, with tech companies reluctant to criticize the government and the government backing extreme anti-regulatory policies. Khan opened an inquiry into AI-cloud partnerships in January 2024.

**What people disagree about.** Whether backing champions wins the race or loses it. Mark Zuckerberg holds that America's advantage is decentralized, open innovation, and wants leading companies working closely with government and allies to keep a first-mover advantage. Alvin Wang Graylin rejects the champion model outright: taxpayers should not provide an implicit federal backstop for the largest concentrated bet in the American economy, and national security arguments should not confer too-big-to-fail status. Tim Wu's main worry is keeping the line between government and powerful private companies; he says no one should be allowed to buy the AI companies and that the giants should be fighting each other at all times.

21:Tf26,**What it is.** The tech companies' move to buy nuclear electricity for data centers, in three forms: long-term power purchase agreements that restart or extend existing reactors, investments in small modular reactors not yet built, and uprates that squeeze more output from plants already running. Nuclear plants put out a constant supply, which matches a data center that wants to run full out around the clock, and Google's Michael Terrell lists the advantages as clean, firm, carbon-free and able to be sited almost anywhere.

**Where it comes from.** The announcements came in a rush from September 2024. Constellation signed a 20-year agreement with Microsoft to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1, an 837-megawatt reactor closed for economic reasons in 2019 and renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center, aiming to be online in 2028 with a license extended to at least 2054; Constellation's chief executive called nuclear the only source that can deliver carbon-free power every hour of every day. In October Google signed with Kairos Power for a fleet of molten-salt small modular reactors, the first deployment by 2030 and 500 megawatts by 2035, the first corporate agreement for multiple deployments of a single advanced reactor design in the United States; Amazon invested in X-energy and agreed to fund the first phase of a small modular reactor project in Washington state that could grow to 960 megawatts in the early 2030s. The Department of Energy guaranteed 1.52 billion dollars to reopen the Palisades plant in Michigan, and Meta's head of energy says relicensing operating plants is the biggest tool available to anyone unwilling to wait a decade. In Europe, Macron offered France's nuclear surplus to data centers with the line plug, baby, plug.

**Why it matters here.** It is the companies' answer to the climate targets they are missing, and the one energy source in the United States with support on both sides of the aisle while renewables are under attack. It also shows the scale of the gap: all US reactors together produced about 800 terawatt-hours in 2022, a figure flat for two decades, and meeting the data-center demand expected in 2030 with nuclear alone would mean expanding the fleet by half. Twenty-four reactors come up for license renewal before 2035, a handful of closed plants could reopen, and uprates could add two to eight gigawatts in total, while OpenAI has talked of single sites needing five gigawatts.

**What people disagree about.** Timing, and what fills the gap. Casey Crownhart's reading in MIT Technology Review is that the companies need power in three to five years and new plants take close to a decade, the small modular reactor developers have not built their first units, and so the nuclear headlines coexist with coal plants kept open and new gas plants that could run for decades; what gets built now stays on the grid through 2040. Terrell himself says nuclear gets a lot of love but wind, solar, storage and geothermal are equally important. The Belfer Center notes that Dominion's plan for Virginia counts small modular reactors among 21 gigawatts of new renewable and nuclear capacity against 5.9 gigawatts of gas, a bet on a technology with no commercial unit yet. The UN University's report adds the warning that low-carbon is not automatically low-water or low-land, so a switch of fuel can move the footprint rather than remove it.

22:Tf96,**What it is.** Generation built or parked beside a data center so it can run before, or instead of, a grid connection: truck-mounted gas turbines, permanent gas plants, diesel generators to absorb the sharp swings in load that training runs produce. In the IEA's base case, gas supplies more than 130 terawatt-hours of additional annual US data-center electricity through 2030, more than renewables, and hyperscale campuses often demand new gas plants and transmission lines of their own. Diesel backup generators, run only in emergencies, emit 200 to 600 times more nitrogen oxides than gas plants, and one Virginia analysis ties even limited backup use to nearly 300 million dollars a year in public health costs; WRI reports more than 30 gas turbines intended for daily use at Colossus.

**Where it comes from.** The case that defined it is Memphis. In 2024 xAI took over a former Electrolux factory on the edge of the Boxtown neighborhood, named it Colossus and filled it with 200,000 Nvidia GPUs on the way to a million. To power it the company moved about 35 mobile methane-gas generators onto the site, many made by Caterpillar, emitting nitrogen oxides and formaldehyde without a permit. The Southern Environmental Law Center said in April 2025 that xAI had built a power plant in South Memphis with no oversight; the mayor said only 15 were running, but volunteer pilots with thermal cameras found at least 33 firing at once, together about 420 megawatts, the output of the Tennessee Valley Authority's nearby gas plant. The surrounding neighborhoods are predominantly Black, already host chemical plants and an oil refinery, and lead the state in emergency visits for asthma. xAI said its turbines carried low-emission and catalytic reduction equipment that cut nitrogen oxides to 2 parts per million. The NAACP sued in June 2025 on the grounds that the turbines were illegally sending pollution into Black neighborhoods, and in June 2026 the Justice Department asked a federal court to quash the case and others like it nationwide.

**Why it matters here.** It is where the abstract electricity question becomes air that people breathe, and it is the fastest route around the constraint that grids take years to expand. Bill McKibben argues that Musk had an alternative, since a 2024 industry report found off-grid solar microgrids a quick and affordable way to power such data centers and called rental gas power a costly one-off that users abandon as soon as they can. Justin Pearson, the state legislator who lives three miles from the site, asks what good money is if the community has to struggle with polluted air, and says solar and batteries would not pump smog-forming chemicals into the neighborhood.

**What people disagree about.** Whether on-site gas is a bridge or a lock-in. Lea Reitmeier and Lutz cite the xAI turbines as a concrete example of AI expanding fossil power and delaying its retirement; Alexis Abramson argues the fossil expansion is overstated and clean generation can meet the growth. Energy Secretary Chris Wright defends keeping aging coal plants open past retirement and dismisses solar because the sun goes down, while an appeals court struck down one such order. The permitting fight is also about who counts: the company and the mayor spoke of exploiting the project for the city, and the health department's town hall gave citizens two minutes each and no answers.

Sources: [[2025-how-is-elon-musk-powering-his-supercomputer?]], [[2026-at-a-times-event,-dueling-visions-on-climate-change-and-a.i.]], [[2024-environmental-impact-of-ai]], [[2025-explained-generative-ai’s-environmental-impact]], [[2025-ai-is-set-to-drive-surging-electricity-demand-from-data-cent]], [[2025-what-direct-risks-does-ai-pose-to-the-climate-and-environmen]], [[2026-could-data-centers-swing-an-election-in-wisconsin?]], [[2026-from-energy-use-to-air-quality-the-many-ways-data-centers-af]], [[2025-naacp-ecj-advocates-release-guiding-principles-to-protect-fr]]
23:Tc17,**What it is.** Open weights are the published parameters of a trained model, the numbers that decide how strongly each input counts in its calculations. Publishing them lets anyone download and run the model; whether they may modify, fine-tune or redistribute it depends on the license. The Open Source Initiative distinguishes open weights from open-source AI, which also releases training code, training data, checkpoints and documentation. Open weights allow local deployment, customization, independent research and competition without the developer's API, but once distributed they cannot be withdrawn and their safeguards can be removed.

**Where it comes from.** Meta made the practice mainstream. Mark Zuckerberg framed it as the Linux story repeating: closed Unix variants lost to an open system that became the foundation of cloud and mobile. Llama 2 in 2023 trailed the frontier; in July 2024 Meta released Llama 3.1 405B as the first frontier-level open model. Zuckerberg's reasons were that Meta does not sell model access, so openness costs it no revenue, and that an ecosystem of tools only forms around a shared model. Yann LeCun put the civic case: assistants will mediate access to knowledge, and that repository cannot be controlled by a handful of companies on the US west coast. Chinese labs then took the lead; DeepSeek has released under free licenses since January 2025.

**Why it matters here.** Open weights have become a lever in the race with China. Chinese companies release under permissive licenses while US labs favor proprietary models at the largest scale. By August 2026 the largest open models, all above a trillion parameters, were Chinese: Kimi K3 at 2.8 trillion, Qwen3.8 at 2.4 trillion, DeepSeek V4 at 1.6 trillion. Alvin Wang Graylin reports that Chinese open-weight models went from under 2% of OpenRouter traffic in late 2024 to a majority among top models, with eight of the top ten by usage open weight in July 2026, and urges US labs to ship competitive open models, since that is where diffusion is decided.

**What people disagree about.** Safety: Zuckerberg argues open models are safer, since most feared harms are unintentional and transparency catches them, and large actors can check small ones if everyone has similar models; the counter-argument is that safeguards can be stripped and releases cannot be recalled, and some US politicians want to restrict access to Chinese tools. Whether it is open at all: DeepSeek shares weights but not training data, and Llama's license obliges companies with more than 700 million users to talk to Meta first. Whether the commitment lasts: Zuckerberg himself worries that rivals dabble in openness only to compete with Meta and that Android shows an open platform closing over time.

24:T67a,**What it is.** Pause Giant AI Experiments: An Open Letter, published by the Future of Life Institute in March 2023, called on all AI labs to immediately pause for at least six months the training of AI systems more powerful than GPT-4, citing AI-generated propaganda, extreme automation of jobs, human obsolescence and a society-wide loss of control. It received more than 30,000 signatures.

**Where it comes from.** It appeared a week after GPT-4's release, argued that large language models were becoming human-competitive at general tasks, and warned of race-to-the-bottom dynamics in which labs skip safety to ship first.

**Why it matters here.** It is the moment the risk argument reached the general public, and the first test of whether the labs would slow down. None paused. Two months later many of their leaders signed the shorter extinction-risk statement instead.

**What people disagree about.** Yudkowsky's TIME reply argued the letter asked for too little: a six-month moratorium would be better than none, but the situation called for shutting it all down, indefinitely and worldwide. LeCun holds the opposite view, that the danger scenarios are built on false assumptions. Helen Toner, who thought it reasonable in 2023 to ask what a six-month pause would achieve, says that by 2026 progress in interpretability and AI control gives a slowdown something to do with the time, though she still doubts an emergency brake would work.

25:Tb3e,**What it is.** On 1 July 2025, which Cloudflare called Content Independence Day, the company changed its default to block AI crawlers unless they pay creators for their content, saying a majority of the world's leading publishers and AI companies joined it. Matthew Prince describes the next step as a marketplace where creators and AI companies of any size meet, and a way of valuing content by how much it fills the holes in an AI engine's knowledge, rather than by the traffic it draws.

**Where it comes from.** Prince's argument starts from Google's original deal, copy our content and we send you traffic, which he says defined the web for thirty years and no longer holds: Google's share of searches is falling for the first time in a decade, answer boxes and AI Overviews keep users on Google, and by Cloudflare's measure AI tools make traffic hundreds or thousands of times harder to earn than the Google of old. His conclusion is that the web is being stripmined by AI crawlers while creators see almost no traffic and almost no value.

**Why it matters here.** It is the first large-scale attempt to replace traffic with payment at the infrastructure layer, and it rests on the empirical dispute over whether AI answers really cut traffic.

**What people disagree about.** The design. Really Simple Licensing, launched in September 2025 by Eckart Walther, a co-author of RSS, with Reddit, Yahoo, People Inc., Medium, Quora and O'Reilly among the first supporters, keeps the gate open but adds machine-readable license terms to robots.txt, from free and attribution to pay-per-crawl and pay-per-inference, and a nonprofit collective to negotiate for publishers the way ASCAP and BMI do for musicians; the Reuters Institute notes the standard cannot block a crawler by itself and relies on AI companies honoring it. At the end of 2025 Digiday's panel of publishers rated the platforms' willingness to pay from Microsoft's pay-per-use marketplace at the top to Anthropic, with no deals and a crawler that flouts robots.txt, at zero. Ben Thompson wants payment inside the protocols of the agentic web rather than at the crawler gate: stablecoin micro-payments and an auction that pays sources by citation, so that a marketplace rather than deals with a few blessed publishers sets the price. Google's position, through Liz Reid, is that websites already control whether and how their content appears in Search through open web protocols, and that Search's value exchange with the web remains strong.

26:Tb76,**What it is.** A phone-free school keeps students away from their phones for the whole school day, not only during lessons. Jonathan Haidt ranks school phone policies on a scale of five. At the first two levels students keep their phones and are told not to use them; at the third they drop them in a classroom caddy each lesson; at the fourth they lock them in a pouch on arrival; at the fifth they leave them in a locker until they go home. He calls the first two nearly useless: only the last two create a phone-free school, because only they give students six or seven hours a day away from the device.

**Where it comes from.** Haidt made the case in June 2023 from visits to his old high school and middle school in Scarsdale, New York, where administrators told him students arrived already anxious, depressed and addicted to their phones. He ties it to an international epidemic of teen mental illness that he and Zach Rausch date to around 2012, when teens moved from flip phones to smartphones. As of 2020, 77 percent of US schools reported phone bans, a figure Haidt reads as an unenforceable wish. France banned phones on school grounds through grade nine in 2018. The US Surgeon General issued an advisory on social media and youth mental health in May 2023.

**Why it matters here.** The evidence Haidt assembles: in a 2016 study, 97 percent of college students said they sometimes use phones in class for non-educational purposes; students who do learn less; and in one experiment, a phone on the desk or in a pocket lowered scores on memory and intelligence tests. Phones also pull students away from one another: Haidt cites a global rise in loneliness at school after 2012 and Sherry Turkle's line that because of our phones we are forever elsewhere. Turkle herself lists the classroom among the sacred spaces where the phone should not be brought. Cal Newport adds that scholars faced information overload from the 1500s, and the answer then, as now, was to focus on one thing at a time.

**What people disagree about.** Whether the evidence justifies the policy. Haidt concedes that many findings are correlational and hopes a governor or superintendent will randomly assign some middle schools to go phone-free a year before others. Opponents cite teaching uses and parents' wish to reach their children; Haidt answers with the school-safety expert Ken Trump's warning that phones distract from instructions during a lockdown. The question now reaches universities: Sian Leah Beilock reports that the University of Chicago Law School has banned all screens from first-year classrooms and warns that prohibition cannot be the only answer to AI, while Haidt banned laptops from his own NYU classes and says his students approved.

27:T937,**What it is.** The process by which AI systems begin autonomously building and improving new generations of more powerful AI at ever more rapid speeds, in Klein's description. Altman's version, in his 2025 essay, is that using AI to do faster AI research is a larval form of it.

**Where it comes from.** The idea is old in the rationalist community, where a sudden takeoff was called the FOOM moment, as Klein put it to Matt Sheehan. Sheehan describes the race metaphor that dominates Silicon Valley and Washington as ending in exactly that: some company or country whose well-aligned model moves into recursive self-improvement first.

**Why it matters here.** It is where the risk and race questions meet. Klein argues in September 2026 that the labs are on the cusp of it and must be stopped, because we lack sufficient control of today's systems to let them build tomorrow's; he cites Amodei writing that it could outrun our ability to understand and control these systems and must be pursued very carefully, if at all, and Anthropic's own warning that misalignment in today's models could compound as they build their successors until control is lost. Helen Toner told Klein a month earlier that automating their own research is the labs' explicit business plan, that it is free of oversight because it releases no product, and that they now post jobs for recursive self-improvement safety engineers, something nobody discussed openly a year or two before; Rogé Karma reports that the companies expect the loop to turn leaps that now come every few months into ones every few weeks or days.

**What people disagree about.** Whether to ban it, and whether a ban could even be defined: Klein reports Altman saying it is very hard to say what a ban on it would mean. And whether the takeoff is an event at all, which is LeCun's objection to the whole picture. Toner's suggestion is cultural: one lab declaring it a bad idea could change what researchers consider acceptable. Klein's observation is that in a single year letting AI write the next AI went from technically impossible to unthinkable not to do.

28:T476,The Silicon Shield is real, but it’s also overrated. Both Washington and Beijing have a strong interest in TSMC continuing to function. Neither side wants to be cut off from advanced chips. China has spent enormous sums trying to build a domestic alternative, with limited success at the leading edge. The U.S. passed the CHIPS Act and is subsidizing TSMC fabs in Arizona and elsewhere. But Taipei has banned TSMC from making its most advanced chips abroad, so the bleeding edge stays on the island for the foreseeable future. That mutual dependence does create a deterrent against the most catastrophic scenarios.

But the Silicon Shield is overrated for two reasons. First, China can “quarantine” Taiwan with its coast guard, conduct customs inspections of every ship leaving Kaohsiung, and choke the island’s economy without ever touching a fab. The chips would still be made — they just couldn’t get out unless China said so.

Second, the U.S. plan to weaponize the Silicon Shield in a crisis — using export controls or the Foreign Direct Product Rule to deny China access to TSMC chips — has serious enforcement problems.29:Td7b,**What it is.** The silicon shield is the idea that Taiwan's chip industry matters so much to the world economy that China would not risk seizing the island by force, and that if it tried, the United States and others would step in to keep the chips flowing. Taiwanese manufacturers made about 60 percent of the world's semiconductors in the early 2020s, TSMC made over 90 percent of the most advanced generation, and China imported more than 100 billion dollars of Taiwanese chips in 2021. Estimates of what a Chinese blockade would cost the world economy run from 2.5 trillion to 5 trillion dollars.

**Where it comes from.** Taiwan's chip industry took off in the 1990s, when TSMC began making chips to American designs, and by 2000 the phrase was appearing in commentary on the economic risks of an invasion. President Tsai Ing-wen described the industry as supporting national security, and her government called it a divine mountain that guards the nation. By the mid-2020s the shield looked weaker: Washington was subsidizing TSMC factories in the United States through the CHIPS Act, Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo called dependence on Taiwanese imports untenable, and Taipei kept the most advanced production at home. The second Trump administration returned to strategic ambiguity in 2025.

**Why it matters here.** Almost all the GPUs that run AI in data centers are made in Taiwan, and Eyck Freymann puts TSMC's share of the chips used to train frontier models at 99 percent. Leopold Aschenbrenner sees an eerie convergence between AGI timelines and the 2027 date by which US officials say China could be ready to invade, so the race to AGI could play out against a Taiwan crisis. Alvin Wang Graylin replies that a Taiwan contingency is a supply chain and alliance problem, not an AGI problem, and that no model capability changes where the fabs sit.

**What people disagree about.** Chris Miller argues the idea gets it backwards: the more disruptive a conflict would be for the US economy, the more Beijing may doubt that Washington would intervene, so dependence emboldens rather than deters, and Germany's bet that gas trade would pacify Russia is the cautionary tale. Christopher McCallion calls it a weak deterrent and a weak incentive at once: Beijing may accept enormous costs to prevent Taiwanese independence, while a captured TSMC would be a hollow prize because China cannot replace the upstream inputs controlled by the US and its allies. Freymann says the shield is real but overrated, since China could quarantine the island with its coast guard and choke its economy without touching a fab, and a US plan to weaponize the shield through export rules faces enforcement problems because chips are routinely transshipped through third countries. Matthew Pottinger has challenged whether the shield exists at all, and Miller told the Council on Foreign Relations in 2023 that he hopes Tsai is right but is not sure.

2a:Td61,**What it is.** Control over the layers AI runs on: the models, the chips and data centers that train and serve them, the clouds that host them, and the data they learn from. Mensch's definition is economic rather than isolationist: sovereignty is leverage, the ability to negotiate with suppliers because you produce some of what you consume, and the retention of the margin that funds the next round of research. Mistral's playbook translates it into measures: a real single market, a European preference in public procurement for strategic sectors, European criteria in the Cloud and AI Development Act, a legal framework for training models in Europe, and a public-domain archive for training data.

**Where it comes from.** Europe's dependence made it concrete. Draghi's figures, over 80% of digital technology imported and three European foundation models against 55 elsewhere, framed the 2024 report; Mensch counts 80% of European digital services as imported from the hyperscalers and warns that the deficit in services will multiply fivefold in five years. The Paris summit in February 2025 turned it into money: Macron's 109 billion euros of private investment and von der Leyen's InvestAI, 200 billion euros with, per the Commission, four gigafactories of about 100,000 chips each, modeled, she said, on CERN. Spain's version is ALIA, 100% publicly funded models in Spanish and the co-official languages trained on MareNostrum 5, which the government presents explicitly as reinforcing Spain's and Europe's technological sovereignty. ASML invested in Mistral in September 2025.

**Why it matters here.** It is the European answer to the question of whether the race has a finish line: not to win it but to stay a producer in it. It also links two other arguments in this atlas, since Mensch's case rests on electricity as the binding constraint and on open-weight models as the tool that decentralizes a market the American labs would otherwise close.

**What people disagree about.** Whether it is achievable without the capital. Mensch concedes Mistral's investors are American because no European fund could write the checks, that its data centers depend on Gulf and American money, and that its gigawatt arrives in 2028 or 2029. Whether regulation helps or hurts it: Zuckerberg and Ek call laws designed to increase European sovereignty self-defeating, Mensch says regulating to defend has never worked, Bradford says the gap is structural and deregulation will not close it. Whether it means protection: Draghi warns against blanket protectionism and national champions while backing European preference in procurement and a concentrated Rapidus-style bet; Mensch wants procurement recycled into European R&D but insists competition stay fierce.

2b:Tc01,**What it is.** Two claims about what a machine that behaves intelligently is doing. In the Internet Encyclopedia's formulation, weak AI grants the fact or prospect of intelligent-acting machines; strong AI says those actions can be real intelligence, that some artificial computation is thought. Searle, who drew the line, put it as simulation against duplication: for weak AI the correct simulation is a model of the mind, for strong AI it really is a mind. Both are logically independent of computationalism, the view that all thought is computation. The phrase weak AI is also used for narrow AI that does one task, and strong AI for general or superhuman intelligence; Searle's strong AI sets no limit on how capable a machine can be.

**Where it comes from.** Searle coined the pair in his 1980 Chinese room paper: according to weak AI the computer is a powerful tool for studying the mind; according to strong AI the appropriately programmed computer literally understands and has cognitive states, and its programs are themselves the explanation. Herbert Simon declared in 1957 that there were now machines that think, learn and create, and John Haugeland wrote that AI wanted machines with minds in the full and literal sense. In later presentations Searle identified strong AI with computer functionalism, and Harnad recast it as computationalism, a position many thinkers actually hold and so worth refuting.

**Why it matters here.** The understanding debate is a quarrel over the strong claim. The Stanford Encyclopedia counts three classic attacks on strong AI: Searle's Chinese room, the Gödelian argument of Lucas and Penrose, and Dreyfus's case that human expertise is not the manipulation of symbols; it also doubts that philosophers could ever overthrow weak AI. Butlin and Long make the strong thesis their working hypothesis under a new name, computational functionalism, because only then does how an AI system works bear on whether it might be conscious.

**What people disagree about.** Whether behavior is evidence of thought. The Internet Encyclopedia's own verdict is that weak AI does not entail strong AI but prima facie it does, and that computers should be credited with thinking when they do what counts as thinking in humans, absent a credible theoretical reason against. Searle's reason is biological: only something with the causal powers of a brain can think, and a simulated rainstorm leaves no one wet. Chalmers calls the biology requirement chauvinism and holds silicon as apt a substrate as carbon, while granting a one-in-three credence that biology is required. Lieto argues that current AI and cognitive modeling sit comfortably within weak AI, using artificial models of the mind without pretending they are the real thing.

Sources: [[1980-searle-minds-brains-and-programs]], [[2026-iep-artificial-intelligence]], [[2026-sep-artificial-intelligence]], [[2026-wikipedia-weak-ai]], [[2026-wikipedia-chinese-room]], [[2023-consciousness-in-artificial-intelligence-insights-from-the-scie]], [[2024-llm-consciousness-bostonreview]]
2c:Ta81,**What it is.** Artificial superintelligence is a hypothetical type of AGI that is much more generally intelligent than humans. The existential-risk hypothesis holds that substantial progress toward it could lead to human extinction or another irreversible global catastrophe, and the debates center on whether AI can gain the needed capabilities, how fast it could improve itself, and whether it can be kept aligned with human values.

**Where it comes from.** Nick Bostrom's 2014 book Superintelligence gave the idea its modern form and the control problem its name. Altman's OpenAI calls itself a superintelligence research company and writes of a takeoff already begun.

**Why it matters here.** Researchers warn that a rapid, recursive cycle of self-improvement could outrun safety measures, especially if companies are racing for the most powerful model, which ties this cluster to the race questions. Hinton frames the stake plainly: we are making things more intelligent than ourselves and have never been in that situation before.

**What people disagree about.** Whether it arrives as an event. LeCun says the assumption that someone will one day find the secret and switch on a machine that takes over the world is false; it will not be an event. Yudkowsky says building it under anything like current conditions most likely kills everyone. Hinton says anyone certain of a takeover is as wrong as anyone certain there will be none, and asks for research on staying in control. Ian Bogost adds a cultural reading: a superintelligence that eradicates civilization is a more fulfilling fear than a cluster of haphazard programs, and the thinkable danger runs through fragile networked infrastructure rather than superhuman intellect. Helen Toner, asked about Zuckerberg's argument that the safe version is everyone having one, says it answers a real problem but assumes an alignment nobody yet knows how to build. In August 2026 Zuckerberg published a letter arguing, in Klein's summary, that the danger is one person having superintelligence and that everyone should have it; by September some politicians, facing a frightened public, were calling for nuclear-style treaties with China and a ban on superintelligence itself.

2d:Tc2c,**What it is.** Tacit knowledge is knowledge that is hard to extract or put into words, as opposed to explicit knowledge that can be written down and handed over. Knowing that London is in the United Kingdom is explicit; riding a bicycle, kneading dough, recognizing a face among a million or judging when a surgical intern is ready are tacit. It is acquired through experience and passed on by close contact, imitation and practice. Michael Polanyi put it in one line: we can know more than we can tell. Gilbert Ryle's distinction between know-how and know-what points the same way.

**Where it comes from.** Ryle argued against the view that all knowledge is knowledge of propositions in a 1945 paper. Polanyi coined tacit knowing in Personal Knowledge in 1958 and developed it in The Tacit Dimension in 1966, holding that all knowledge is rooted in it. Ikujiro Nonaka and Hirotaka Takeuchi turned it into a management model in the 1990s, illustrated by the Matsushita engineer who apprenticed herself to a master baker in 1985 to mechanize dough kneading. Harry Collins returned to the distinction in Tacit and Explicit Knowledge in 2010.

**Why it matters here.** The concept sits under two live questions. On jobs: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen find that since ChatGPT, employment has fallen among young workers in occupations that rely on codified knowledge, taught through textbooks and procedures, and risen among experienced workers in occupations built on tacit knowledge, consistent with generative AI reproducing what is already encoded in text while experience stays harder to copy. On the race: Leopold Aschenbrenner rejects the argument that tacit knowledge would stop China competing even if it stole the secrets, since Chinese labs have shown they can train large models and the recipe can be conveyed in an hour. Sarah Myers West notes that making the most of scarce hardware needs tacit knowledge too, which makes talent a barrier to entry.

**What people disagree about.** Whether AI can absorb tacit knowledge at all. Brynjolfsson, Danielle Li and Lindsey Raymond argue that tasks which defied automation because they could not be codified, such as knowing what tone is appropriate, are now within reach, because machine learning infers instructions from examples; their study of 5,172 customer support agents found AI assistance lifted productivity by 15% and made lower-skill agents write more like top performers. The same Brynjolfsson, in the Canaries work, treats tacit knowledge as the shelter experienced workers still have, while stressing that the patterns are descriptive, not causal. And whether the line is clean: the management literature describes tacit knowledge both as uncodifiable and as something to codify, and some philosophers hold that all propositional knowledge reduces to practical knowledge.

Sources: [[2026-wikipedia-tacit-knowledge]], [[2026-no-widespread-displacement-but-the-ai-employment-gap-for-you]], [[2024-2304-11771]], [[2024-iiid-the-free-world-must-prevail-situational-awareness]], [[2023-computational-power-and-ai-comment-submission]]
2e:Tbc3,**What it is.** Turing's proposal to judge a machine by conversation. In the modern version a human evaluator reads a text exchange between a person and a machine and tries to identify the machine; it passes if the evaluator cannot reliably tell them apart. Turing framed it as an imitation game: an interrogator questions a man and a woman by written notes and tries to say which is which, and then a machine takes the man's place. The point was to replace the question of whether machines can think with one expressed in relatively unambiguous words. Harnad's Total Turing Test adds perception and the handling of objects.

**Where it comes from.** Turing's 1950 paper Computing Machinery and Intelligence opens by proposing to consider whether machines can think. He had described a paper chess machine in a 1948 report and gave a jury version on the BBC in 1952. Descartes had drawn the line at the same place in 1637: an automaton could utter words but never arrange its speech to reply appropriately to everything said in its presence. Turing predicted that in about fifty years an average interrogator would have no more than a 70 percent chance of a correct identification after five minutes; by 2000, at the Loebner Prize, the figure was 100 percent.

**Why it matters here.** The test is the behaviourist answer to the atlas's understanding question, and Searle built the Chinese room to show that two systems can both pass it while only one understands. Bender and Koller argue that a system trained on form alone would fail a sufficiently sensitive version because it cannot connect its words to the world. Butlin and Long reject behavioral tests for consciousness altogether, since AI systems can be trained to mimic human behavior while working in very different ways. Brynjolfsson sees a Turing Trap: by rewarding imitation of humans over augmentation, the test steers technology toward substituting for workers.

**What people disagree about.** Whether passing means anything now that models pass. In March 2024 Stanford researchers reported that ChatGPT-4 passes a rigorous version, diverging from human behavior mainly by being more cooperative, and a 2025 study found GPT-4.5, told to adopt a persona, judged human 73 percent of the time, more often than the real participants. Marcus insists the test only shows how easy it is to fool people. Russell and Norvig note that aeronautics does not aim to build planes that fool pigeons. Chalmers says many take it as a sufficient condition for consciousness though not a necessary one. ELIZA fooled people in 1966 knowing almost nothing of the world; the interrogator matters as much as the machine.

Sources: [[2026-wikipedia-turing-test]], [[2026-iep-artificial-intelligence]], [[2026-sep-artificial-intelligence]], [[1980-searle-minds-brains-and-programs]], [[2020-climbing-towards-nlu-on-meaning-form-and-understanding-in-th]], [[2023-consciousness-in-artificial-intelligence-insights-from-the-scie]], [[2024-llm-consciousness-bostonreview]]
2f:T5c9,**What it is.** Water withdrawn and consumed by AI, both directly, to cool the servers, and indirectly, in the power plants that supply their electricity. Ren and colleagues distinguish scope-1 water, on site, from scope-2 water, embedded in electricity, and project the two together for global AI at 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic meters in 2027, four to six times Denmark's annual withdrawal.

**Where it comes from.** The paper Making AI Less Thirsty, from researchers at UC Riverside, was the first to estimate AI's water footprint from public data, in 2023. Crawford's Nature comment the following year brought the companies' own figures into view.

**Why it matters here.** Water is local in a way electricity is not: a data center draws on one district's supply. Crawford reports a cluster in West Des Moines, Iowa, serving GPT-4, that used about 6 percent of the district's water in July 2022, a figure that surfaced only through a residents' lawsuit, and year-on-year water increases of 20 percent at Google and 34 percent at Microsoft as they built their chatbots.

**What people disagree about.** Less the physics than the accounting: withdrawal against consumption, on-site against embedded, and above all whether the companies should have to report it. Ren's title calls the footprint secret; Crawford says the costs are mostly secret and calls for disclosure.

30:T12eb,**What it is.** The allocation of the cost of new generation, transmission and substations between the data centers that trigger it and the ratepayers and taxpayers around them. Utilities recover infrastructure through rates set over decades; a data center can stop paying long before the assets are amortized. The instruments on the developer's side are large-load tariffs, which several US states have created, and laws requiring developers to bear the cost of new energy infrastructure, which California, Ohio and Utah were the first to pass among at least 27 states considering data center legislation in 2026. The instruments on the other side are tax exemptions and electricity rates that spread the cost.

**Where it comes from.** The forecasts made it a public question. London Economics found that utilities plan for demand that may never arrive, since developers file the same project with several utilities and a former Google engineer counted five to ten times more interconnection requests than data centers built; Virginia's auditors put the bill for typical Dominion households at 14 to 37 dollars a month by 2040. Wisconsin wrote sales and use tax exemptions for data centers into its 2023 budget, including on electricity and with no sunset, at a cost its fiscal bureau puts above 2 billion dollars; its public service commission expects generation needs to rise 40 percent in six years, largely from data centers. The federal tax bill of 2025 has given six AI-invested companies nearly 83 billion dollars in tax breaks. Oregon's regulator approved a large-load tariff framework in May 2026 that makes data centers pay for their grid upgrades. The Belfer Center's grid brief adds the reliability side: in July 2024 a voltage fluctuation in northern Virginia disconnected 60 data centers at once, leaving a 1,500-megawatt surplus that forced emergency adjustments, and Dominion proposed its first base-rate increase since 1992 in 2025, about 8.51 dollars a month for a typical household in 2026. Texas answered with Senate Bill 6 in June 2025, which directs its utility commission to set a reasonable share of upgrade costs for new large loads and requires disclosure to cut speculative filings; AEP Ohio now makes data centers pay for at least 85 percent of the energy they subscribe to whether or not they use it, and Minnesota and Missouri have created billing classes for large users.

**Why it matters here.** It is the one point on which the two parties' candidates agree: in Wisconsin both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor say corporations should cover the costs of upgrading the grid, nondisclosure agreements should be banned and communities should be able to refuse. Developers now lead with it: in Clinton, Iowa, the Blackstone-owned developer asked for no incentives and promised to pay for all utility improvements, and the utility promised existing customers would not pay. Opponents answer with the Foxconn precedent, 4.5 billion dollars of subsidy for a factory that never employed more than about a thousand people, part of whose land Microsoft is now turning into 17 data centers.

**What people disagree about.** Whether the promises hold when the demand does not. Jonathan Koomey warns that forecasts beyond a few years are guesswork; Cory Doctorow expects GPUs at ten cents on the dollar after the bubble; Annie Lowrey counts 1,500 data centers under construction and bond issuance above 250 billion dollars. If the capacity is built and the tenants leave, the question of who pays answers itself. The other dispute is about transparency: Greenpeace and local organizers argue that the costs are hidden by nondisclosure agreements and by state commissions that approve plants without local input, while supporters say property taxes, 20 to 30 million dollars a year in Clinton's case, are the point. The Union of Concerned Scientists puts the electricity costs attributable to data centers at nearly a trillion dollars over 25 years and argues they must pay a fair share; the Belfer authors note that contract-based financing through special tariffs and power purchase agreements has moved projects away from transparent rate-base recovery and may shift costs onto other consumers.

Sources: [[2024-environmental-impact-of-ai]], [[2026-wikipedia-data-center]], [[2025-general]], [[2026-could-data-centers-swing-an-election-in-wisconsin?]], [[2026-the-great-data-center-rebellion]], [[2026-the-energy-and-environmental-impact-of-ai-and-how-it-undermi]], [[2026-the-ai-bubble-is-no-ordinary-bubble]], [[2026-data-centers-are-a-distraction]], [[2025-bpc-report-electricity-demand-growth-and-data-centers-a-guid]], [[2026-ai-data-centers-and-the-u-s-electric-grid-a-watershed-moment]], [[2026-data-center-power-play]], [[2026-from-energy-use-to-air-quality-the-many-ways-data-centers-af]]
31:Tc9e,**What it is.** An internal model of how the world changes, including as a result of one's own actions. In LeCun's account a world model takes the state of the world at time T and an action, and predicts the state at T plus one; it need not represent everything, only what matters for planning. Building one means observing the world and understanding why it evolves as it does. The idea descends from the mental model of psychology, an internal representation of external reality, and experiments in weightlessness and with neuroimaging show that people carry one for how gravity moves objects.

**Where it comes from.** Kenneth Craik coined the term mental model in his 1943 book The Nature of Explanation, suggesting that the mind builds small-scale models of reality to anticipate events. Philip Johnson-Laird's Mental Models and a collection edited by Gentner and Stevens, both from 1983, carried it into cognitive science. In AI, LeCun's 2022 proposal for autonomous intelligence includes a world model for planning, and his Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture, JEPA, predicts abstract representations of video rather than every pixel, after a decade of failed generative video prediction. Hassabis, who studied how the brain does imagination, calls it mental simulation and asks how the brain constructs the right world models.

**Why it matters here.** Whether current models have one is a fork in the understanding debate. LeCun names understanding the physical world, persistent memory, reasoning and planning as the four essentials of intelligence, says language models do none of them or only primitively, and holds that a world model cannot be built by predicting words because language carries too little information. Hassabis calls ever more reliable world models a necessary but probably insufficient component of AGI, to be topped with AlphaZero-style planning; the better the model, he says, the less search it needs. Mitchell and Krakauer put the contrast at the center of the debate: mental models built from statistical correlations against models built on causal mechanisms.

**What people disagree about.** Whether prediction on text can produce one. Chalmers argues that minimizing prediction error may require world models, as maximizing fitness produced eyes and wings, and cites Kenneth Li's Othello study as evidence that a sequence model built an internal map of the 64 squares, while conceding that they look fragile and self-models poorer still. Mitchell and Krakauer ask whether these systems build anything like the concept-based mental models of human understanding or only correlations that mimic them. LeCun bets the next world models will be JEPA-like rather than generative, notes that learned hierarchical planning has zero demonstrations in AI, and expects the program to take at least a decade and probably much more.

32:T840,**What it is.** A zero-click result is a web query the user resolves on the search engine results page without navigating to any other source. Because nothing is requested from the publisher's server, standard web analytics record nothing, so marketing built on pageviews cannot see it.

**Where it comes from.** From the late 2000s search platforms began filling their results pages with content scraped from the sites they indexed: Universal Search in 2007, rich snippets in 2009, then knowledge panels. Nilay Patel of The Verge coined "Google Zero" in 2024 for the point at which Google stops sending any clicks at all; Wired's Katie Drummond called the phenomenon a traffic apocalypse, and both publications have turned to newsletters and direct relationships with readers in response.

**Why it matters here.** The figures set the baseline for the AI dispute. A SparkToro study of 2024 put zero-click searches at 58.5% of the total, split between queries answered by a knowledge panel or snippet and queries that ended in another search; as of 2025 about 60% of US search users do not leave the search platform. Matthew Prince cites research that 75% of mobile queries were answered without leaving Google once the answer box arrived, and says AI Overviews push the figure higher.

**What people disagree about.** Whether AI answers add a new kind of zero click or merely continue an old one: Liz Reid points out that quick answers like the date of the next full moon have long been satisfied by features such as the Knowledge Graph, while Pew's data show users ending their session more often after an AI summary than after a plain results page. Clara Soteras argues the zero click is not new, and what changed in 2025 is which content it reaches: evergreen explainers that Google can already answer.

3d:Tc6a,## Why it is open

Nobody agrees on what would count, so the same year of releases is read as arrival and as a wall. The lab leaders give the earliest dates. Dario Amodei avoids the term and talks about powerful AI, which he wrote in 2024 could come as early as 2026, though there are ways it could take much longer. Sam Altman said in January 2025 that OpenAI was confident it knew how to build AGI as traditionally understood, and later that year that humanity is past the event horizon and the takeoff toward digital superintelligence has started, with 2026 likely to bring systems that find novel insights and 2027 perhaps robots that do real-world tasks. Demis Hassabis gives no number because of the many unknowns, but says DeepMind's twenty-year plan from 2010 is on track and he would not be surprised by AGI-like systems within the decade.

The skeptics divide by reason. Gary Marcus reads 2025's setbacks, the Apple reasoning paper and GPT-5's shortfall, as proof that large language models are not the road to AGI and that anyone expecting the current paradigm to be close is deluded. Ilya Sutskever, who helped build the scaling era, says it is over: pre-training data is finite, the field is back in the age of research, and a system that learns as well as a human and then becomes superhuman is five to twenty years away. Emma Pierson reports that most experts in a forecasting survey she advised expect slower progress than the lab leaders, and argues that domains like cancer, unlike chess or coding, cannot be experimented on at silicon speed; she roots for delays because AI's broader effects are already arriving faster than institutions can handle.

What keeps the question open is that the definition is loose enough to absorb any outcome. Amodei's powerful AI, Altman's takeoff, Hassabis's AGI-like systems and Sutskever's superhuman learner are four different thresholds, and the lab definitions are economic, outperforming humans at valuable work, while the skeptics' tests are about learning and reasoning. Each side can point to the same releases as evidence.

3e:Te38,## Why it is open

The evidence points in two directions at once, and the forecasts span everything from modest to total. On the data, the Yale Budget Lab finds no discernible economy-wide disruption in the first 33 months after ChatGPT and notes that past technologies took decades to reshape work. Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen find the same absence of mass displacement but a widening gap for the young: employment of 22 to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs runs about 19 percent behind their less-exposed peers, up from 15 percent a year earlier, mainly through less hiring and concentrated where AI automates rather than complements. They stress the pattern is suggestive, not proof that AI is the cause.

On the forecasts, Daron Acemoglu's 2024 paper puts AI's gain in total factor productivity at no more than 0.66 percent over ten years, probably less, because early gains come from easy-to-learn tasks, and predicts a wider gap between capital and labor income; by 2026 he was arguing that generative AI could supercharge four decades of inequality unless development is redirected toward pro-worker AI. Dario Amodei predicts that AI will disrupt about half of entry-level white-collar jobs within one to five years even as it speeds growth, while agreeing it is likely not displacing jobs yet. Bill Gates calls mass job losses inevitable unless addressed, concedes that past breakthroughs created more jobs than they destroyed, and stakes everything he knows on this time being different, proposing that roles such as caregiving be reserved for humans. Jensen Huang calls the job-destruction claim a fallacy hardened into a harmful myth: every job will change and single-task jobs such as phone customer service may go, but new industries will bring a net creation of jobs. Elon Musk says that within a decade AI will make people so prosperous that money will not matter.

Cory Doctorow reframes the question as one about bosses rather than machines: AI cannot do your job, but an AI salesman can convince your boss to replace you with it, and when the bubble bursts the AI will be switched off and no one will be doing the work. The question stays open because the early data are consistent with all three readings, a slow transformation on the historical pattern, a fast one that has only begun with the young, or a sales cycle that displaces workers before the technology can replace them.

3f:Tf38,## Why it is open

The mechanism is disputed. Nicholas Carr's version is that the threat is not cheating but the removal of learning: an essay produced without the reading, synthesizing and writing gives students the illusion of having learned while they learn less, and the deskilling then reaches the use of the tool itself, since writing a good prompt requires already knowing the subject. Cal Newport's interviews found students using the chatbot to talk about their writing rather than to write it, which lowered the peak mental strain of the work; that is fine for office email, he argues, and harmful in a classroom, where strain is often a by-product of getting smarter. Thomas Chatterton Williams sees the result in his undergraduates: letting the technology shoulder the burden of thought atrophies the ability to sustain mental effort.

The other side argues that schools adapt and that the tool can teach. Ethan Mollick recalls that parents in the 1970s feared calculators would make children dependent and that math education reached a practical consensus by the 1990s; AI will not replace the need to learn to write and think, and AI tutors can make active learning cheaper to provide. Gregory Kestin's Harvard trial supplies the evidence for that half: a tutor engineered to manage cognitive load and scaffold problems beat an active-learning class, though his team warns against settings where students use AI as a crutch to bypass critical thinking. Sian Leah Beilock argues that universities should give students structured practice with AI rather than ban it, because employers will expect the skill.

The empirical record is early. The MIT Media Lab's EEG study of essay writing found that people using an AI assistant showed the weakest brain connectivity of three groups and underperformed over four months at neural, linguistic and behavioral levels, but its authors call it preliminary and it is not peer-reviewed. An MIT working group's 2026 report names the risk of cognitive surrender and recommends against relying on AI detectors; Turnitin found some AI writing in nearly half of US student submissions in the past academic year, and colleges are split over what to do about it, with one Wisconsin professor who caught 60 AI-written essays in a single assignment planning to scrap writing assignments altogether.

40:Tfcc,## Why it is open

The answer depends on three numbers nobody has pinned down: how much electricity AI will use, what will generate it, and how much emissions AI will help cut elsewhere. On the first, the IEA expects data-center demand to more than double to 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, with AI the main driver, and reported electricity consumption from AI data centers surging 50 percent in a single year; the United Nations University projects AI data centers using nearly three times the electricity of Nigeria, Pakistan and Bangladesh combined by 2030; Greenpeace Germany's scenario has AI data-center demand 11 times higher in 2030 than in 2023 without intervention. Jonathan Koomey reads the national data as showing no explosion yet, and the IEA itself calls data centers a small share of global demand growth. Sasha Luccioni's measurements show that general-purpose generative models cost orders of magnitude more energy per task than task-specific ones, so much of the demand is a design choice, while Sam Altman puts a query at 0.34 watt-hours and expects intelligence to cost little more than the electricity behind it, which would make demand almost unbounded.

On the second, the IEA says fossil fuels supply nearly 60 percent of data-center power today, flipping to 60 percent clean by 2035 in its central case while gas still doubles; MIT's Noman Bashir says the pace of construction means the bulk of new power must come from fossil plants, that generative clusters draw seven or eight times the power of ordinary computing, and that inference will come to dominate. The US administration is keeping coal plants open and throttling wind and solar, and companies are becoming major energy buyers of both renewable and fossil projects, with nuclear the preferred headline: Microsoft's Three Mile Island restart, Google's Kairos reactors and Amazon's X-energy project, none of which deliver before 2028 and most not before the 2030s. The UN University finds inference already 80 to 90 percent of AI's energy use, with ChatGPT's 2.5 billion daily prompts drawing about 383 gigawatt-hours a year. On the third, Eric Horvitz argues the indirect effects could dwarf the direct footprint, Fatih Birol says how AI is used is up to societies and governments, and a 2026 review found most industry claims about climate benefits unproven.

Whether AI speeds the transition or slows it is therefore a question about who buys the power and under what rules. The companies that promised carbon-free operations by 2030 are now the largest new source of demand, and the chip and model efficiency gains that Google reports, a 33-fold cut per prompt in a year, feed into a build-out that grows faster than they save.

41:T1739,## Why it is open

The two sides measure different things. Liz Reid, head of Google Search, wrote in August 2025 that total organic click volume from Google to websites has been relatively stable year on year, that quality clicks are slightly up, and that third-party reports of dramatic declines rest on flawed methods, isolated examples or changes that predate AI features. Pew Research Center, tracking the browsing of 900 US adults in March 2025, found that users who saw an AI summary clicked a traditional result in 8% of visits against 15% for those who did not, clicked a link inside the summary in 1% of visits, and ended their browsing session more often. Chartbeat data gathered for the Reuters Institute show Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 news sites down by a third worldwide between November 2024 and November 2025, and by 38% in the United States, though the report cautions that it is not clear how much of that is AI Overviews, which have largely spared hard news; publishers surveyed expect search traffic to fall by 43% in three years. A natural experiment settles part of the dispute: comparing English Wikipedia articles with the same articles in German and French, where AI Overviews arrived later, researchers estimate that the summaries cut English search referrals by about 5%. Matthew Prince of Cloudflare argues that the content-for-traffic deal Google made thirty years ago no longer makes sense: by Cloudflare's measure it has become about ten times harder to earn traffic from Google than a decade ago, 750 times harder with OpenAI and 30,000 times harder with Anthropic, because people consume derivatives instead of originals. Cory Doctorow says Google now extracts all of the value from the sites it summarizes and gives nothing back, after its own advertising and ranking choices degraded both search and the web it indexes. Ben Thompson sees every leg of the stool that held up the ad-supported web wobbling: readers take the answer, advertisers prefer walled gardens, and Google may lose its motive to support the open web at all.

Even when a reader wants the source, AI search often fails to deliver it. The Tow Center at Columbia tested eight AI search tools with 1,600 queries in early 2025 and found them wrong more than 60% of the time at naming the article, the publisher and the URL, rarely admitting uncertainty, citing syndicated copies instead of originals, fabricating links, and in some cases answering from sites that had blocked their crawlers; a licensing deal with the publisher did not make citations more accurate. Google answered the pressure in December 2025 with more inline links in AI Mode, a global rollout of Preferred Sources and a carousel for a reader's own subscriptions, and said it sends billions of clicks a day.

The Spanish evidence points to a split rather than a uniform collapse. A study of twelve Spanish news sites from January to September 2025 led by M. J. Cachón found that 20.5% of the searches that used to send clicks to them are now answered by Google's AI, that news sites are 3.2 times more exposed than other sectors, and that technology and science and opinion sections fell hardest while economics and sport held up; El Confidencial, Eldiario.es and El Mundo were among the better performers, and the authors conclude that editorial quality protects a site because original, contextual work is harder to synthesize. Clara Soteras argues that the damage is concentrated in niche sites and evergreen content that Google can already answer, while breaking news is less affected, and that Spanish media can no longer be measured by traffic volume at all.
