42:Ta89,## Why it is open

A bubble is only visible from the far side. Cahn's arithmetic is simple: take Nvidia's run-rate revenue forecast, double it for the rest of the data-center cost and double it again for the margin the buyers need, and compare the 600 billion dollars that yields with what AI products earn; in 2024 he put the gap at 500 billion, and OpenAI was the only company with revenue to speak of. The other side of the argument is that the infrastructure is being built for a demand that is real but early, which is what every railway and fiber boom also said. The 2026 reporting shows both at once: Stargate's 500 billion dollar plan and Oracle's debt on one side, and corporate customers discovering they cannot tell what they are buying on the other.

Annie Lowrey and Cory Doctorow, writing in the summer of 2026, agree it is a bubble and disagree about its shape. For Lowrey it is an unusual one, stoked by rich corporations rather than households and inflated on expensive credit, so it may be sturdier and last longer; she counts it as two overlapping bubbles, in capital spending and in valuations. For Doctorow it is the biggest of a string of bubbles that began with a growth story monopolists needed, and it ends where the material limits, chips and energy, bite.

43:T1ce2,## Why it is open

The argument has three layers. The first is factual: how far ahead the American labs are and for how long. Gregory C. Allen judges US firms still ahead but says the gap has narrowed sharply and that even very aggressive export controls cannot secure a lead of more than a year or two; by September 2026 Rogé Karma was reporting experts putting it at about six months and closing, and Epoch AI data showed the gap had not widened despite US chip spending. Matt Sheehan adds a counterweight: China runs on perhaps an eighth or a tenth of US compute. Helen Toner argues the lead may not be securable at all, since Chinese companies distil American models and Chinese state hackers could steal them outright; Anthropic accused DeepSeek of distillation in February 2026 and Alibaba in June, and OpenAI had accused DeepSeek a year earlier.

The second is conceptual: whether AI has a finish line. Leopold Aschenbrenner says it does, that superintelligence would give whoever leads a decisive military advantage, possibly even against nuclear deterrents, and that the United States must win. Alvin Wang Graylin and Paul Triolo answer that there is no finish line and no moat: capability gaps now last months, models are becoming interchangeable commodities, and the race frame justifies vast spending and exemptions from oversight without buying a durable lead. Matteo Wong argues the winner-takes-all framing obscures the stakes, since it assumes a superintelligence that may never be built, while the more plausible threat is an economic race the US could lose slowly. Sheehan says the race-to-superintelligence model is not even China's paradigm; Grace Shao has never heard Chinese executives describe their work as a national contest; and Sarah Myers West notes that the arms-race idea has been wielded since the 2010s to head off regulation. Karma draws the opposite conclusion from the same premises: because the labs will never unilaterally disarm and Chinese firms a few months behind would surpass a throttled US industry, the only way to slow AI is a US-China nonproliferation treaty capping training chips, enforced through data-center inspections.

DeepSeek changed the evidence for both sides. Its January 2025 models came close to the leading US systems while trained largely on export-restricted chips; within two months the share of global web traffic to Chinese models jumped from about 3 to 13 percent, and by July 2026 Z.ai's GLM-5.2 was hailed in Silicon Valley as the first Chinese model to match the top US models at several times lower cost. Analysts read this either as proof that export controls failed or that they worked and China innovated around them. The second shift is open weights: Chinese labs release under permissive licenses while US labs keep their largest models proprietary, and by August 2026 the largest open models, Kimi K3, Qwen3.8 and DeepSeek V4, were all Chinese, with eight of the top ten models by usage on OpenRouter open weight. Graylin's conclusion is that diffusion, not the frontier, is where the contest is decided. Washington's own conduct cuts across the rhetoric: it lifted the ban on Nvidia's H200 in December 2025, which the Institute for Progress estimated could shrink a 20-to-50-fold US compute lead to almost nothing, while Trump dismissed regulation because whoever wins AI wins. In Beijing, Dario Amodei's call for a slowdown is read as a Cold War playbook, and Xi Jinping has said oversight may be needed to forestall loss of control; Ezra Klein doubts Chinese labs will be more reckless than American ones.

44:Teb6,## Why it is open

Three disputes stack up. The first is about pace: Aviv Ovadya, who helped test GPT-4 before its release, said in 2023 that a regulatory system would need to be international and that he did not see existing government institutions navigating it at the rate necessary. The second is about the race: Trump dismissed calls for regulation in September 2026 on the grounds that whoever wins AI wins, and Rogé Karma answers that Trump's own chip policy makes the Chinese threat worse and that the way out is a mutual deceleration agreed with China rather than an anything-goes arms race. Sarah Myers West traces the tactic further back: since the 2010s the idea of a technological arms race has been wielded deliberately to head off regulation of the tech sector. The third is about whether new law is needed at all: Lina Khan argued that enforcers already have authority to charge companies for dangerous or defective products, and Jonathan Chait replies that the dangers are being developed under those laws right now, which suggests they are not sufficient. China shows the opposite concern: some of the world's tightest restrictions on the technology, set by the government with companies complying, alongside the world's largest digital police state.

45:T1aed,## Why it is open

Four parties claim the agent. Stripe and OpenAI describe ChatGPT as the buyer's agent, carrying the shopper's identity, payment and context into the transaction, and their Agentic Commerce Protocol promises merchants that they keep control of what is sold, how their brand appears and their customer relationships. Amazon's lawyers told Perplexity in October 2025 that agents shopping on its store must operate transparently, that Comet may not pick the best price, delivery or recommendations for the customer, that it puts customer data at risk, and that Perplexity had disguised Comet as Google Chrome and circumvented a block within a day; Amazon's public statement compared agents to food delivery apps and travel agencies, which operate openly and respect a provider's decision whether to take part. Perplexity replied in a blog post that users love the experience and that Amazon is more interested in serving ads, sponsored results and upsells than in easier shopping; Amazon's chief executive Andy Jassy said the company was having conversations and might partner with third-party agents if the customer experience is good. In August 2026 the Ninth Circuit vacated the injunction Amazon had won, holding that the Assistant is a tool, not a person, so it is the user who accesses Amazon's computers; the panel kept the holding narrow and noted Amazon can still police access through its terms of service. Eric Goldman reads the ruling as proof that courts still do not know who takes the legally significant actions online, and expects the fight to move to users and to other legal theories.

Brands are the third claimant. Oguz Acar and David Schweidel describe three modes, a brand's own agent talking to customers, a consumer's agent shopping across brands, and agents on both sides with no human in the loop, and argue that consumers trust the agents they control as unbiased advocates, "much like financial advisers with fiduciary duty", while brand agents are suspected of serving the company; they expect pay-to-play placement in agent recommendations to follow the pattern of search advertising. Consumer Reports' Dazza Greenwood says the most compelling use of a personal agent is to advocate for the consumer without bias or conflicting interests, and the organization is exploring agents built to put user interests first. Mikey Vu and colleagues read the same shift as the aggregator story repeating: agents widen a vendor's reach but compress margins and will extract more of the value, so vendors face a prisoner's dilemma and should own the checkout, keep some inventory exclusive and strike data-sharing deals while they still have leverage. Jafar Sabbah and Acar's simulations suggest the agent is not a pushover either way: across four models and 16,000 choices only star ratings and price moved agents consistently, and the more capable models penalized scarcity badges and urgency cues as signs of manipulation.

The fourth claimant is the platform itself. Mark Zuckerberg describes Meta's goal as the ultimate business agent: a business states its objective, connects its bank account and lets Meta's AI produce the creative, choose the audience and measure the results, which he expects to raise advertising's share of GDP; he also wants Meta AI to be a personal AI that knows what the feed algorithm knows about you. Brady Brickner-Wood spent a weekend with Meta's consumer agent Muse, which asks for e-mail, bank, card and social accounts and promises it is working exclusively for you; he refused it the important ones, watched it fumble a reservation, and concluded that what feels like liberation is a new captivity. Tim Berners-Lee's answer is a different kind of agent: Charlie, imagined in 2017, works for Bob "legally, ethically and algorithmically", gets all of Bob's data because Bob trusts him, and is bound like a doctor or a lawyer by law and codes of conduct; the web's inventor argues the frameworks already exist and that power must not again rest with the monopolies that harvest personal data. Cal Newport adds a limit on what any agent can do for you: an e-mail agent is a software layer on top of a commercial model, and it stalls at messages that depend on the tacit knowledge of your life that no prompt can carry. Forrester's Emily Pfeiffer and Sucharita Kodali counter that the whole field is experimental: consumers use answer engines to research products and rarely to buy, OpenAI shelved native checkout within six months, and merchants should hold on to the checkout moment rather than cede it to any engine.

46:Te6a,## Why it is open

The companies still hold their targets and their own reports show the numbers moving the wrong way. Microsoft committed in 2020 to be carbon negative by 2030 and reported in 2024 that emissions across all scopes were up 29 percent against that baseline, naming the infrastructure behind AI and saying the moonshot had become harder. Google announced a carbon-free-by-2030 plan the same year, which Sundar Pichai called a sustainability moonshot and tied to the flooding of his hometown in Chennai; its 2024 report attributed a 13 percent rise in 2023 emissions to data-center energy and supply-chain emissions, and by 2026 both companies' emissions were still rising. Simon Stiell, the UN climate chief, told Climate Week in September 2026 that AI is for now mostly heating pollution from coal, oil and gas while raising energy costs, called the industry energy guzzling and said it must start aligning with global climate efforts urgently; the Turkish presidency of the November 2026 climate conference put AI's energy consumption on the agenda.

Whether the rise is a temporary bulge before clean power catches up, or the shape of the decade, is what the reports cannot say. Kate Crawford's charge is about disclosure: the industry has downplayed and hidden its costs for years, Altman's answer to the energy crisis, nuclear fusion, will not arrive in time to matter, and without mandated reporting nobody outside can check. The claims on the other side of the ledger have the same problem: a February 2026 review backed by Beyond Fossil Fuels found 74 percent of industry claims about AI's climate benefits unproven, and the French Senate concluded in September 2026 that the potential has yet to be realized. The political context has moved too: the Trump administration has withdrawn from the Paris Agreement, orders coal plants kept open and throttles renewables, and Bill Gates, who argued in 2025 that climate change would not end humanity, published an essay on AI risk the following year.

The question stays open because the targets are dated 2030 and the build-out is dated now. Annie Lowrey counts more than 700 billion dollars of spending by Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta in a single year; the IEA expects fossil fuels to supply nearly 60 percent of data-center power today and clean sources 60 percent by 2035 in its central case, with gas still doubling. On those numbers the companies can miss 2030 and still claim the trend.

47:T659,## Why it is open

The historical case for compute is strong: general methods that can absorb more computation repeatedly displaced hand-built systems, and recent frontier models improve as training and inference scale. Yet compute is not an idea by itself. Large runs depend on architectures, algorithms, data curation and experiments that reveal how to use the hardware. Access to compute may decide who can test ideas at the frontier without deciding which ideas will work.

48:T1ad4,## Why it is open

The opposition is wide, fast and cross-party, and nobody is sure what it is about. Nearly 70 percent of Americans oppose a data center in their area, according to an NBC poll in September 2026; a Gallup poll found more than 70 percent; in Wisconsin, Marquette's poll went from 55 percent opposed in October 2025 to 78 percent in August 2026, with 94 percent of Democrats and rising numbers of Republicans. More than 500 jurisdictions have passed moratoriums or bans, New York became the first state to enact one in July 2026, and Rogé Karma counts state moratoriums in Texas too. George Packer, reporting from Clinton, Iowa, where a Blackstone-owned developer planned ten buildings on 1,100 acres under a code name and nondisclosure agreements, found residents citing water, grid capacity, soil, low-frequency noise and light, but concluded that the crux was a feeling of being misled, ignored and disrespected, of having no say over basic matters in their own lives; the steering committee of the opposition group was mostly Republican and would not discuss politics. Dan Kaufman found the same in Rock County, Wisconsin, where a supervisor won conservative precincts purely on the issue and told him people did not get a vote on social media and want one on AI; a Democratic candidate there called data centers the physical target of a visceral populist anger whose real object is AI itself.

The other side argues money and trade-offs. Clinton's mayor said the project could bring 20 million dollars a year in property taxes to a city with a 24 million dollar budget; the developer requested no incentives and promised to pay for all utility improvements, and the regulated utility promised that costs would not fall on existing customers. President Trump said that as a mayor or governor he would absolutely want a data center, because the jobs and the taxes are enormous, and derided opponents as wanting to remain backwards and poor. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the administration is not imposing data centers on anyone and that the positives may be much bigger than the negatives. Supporters in Clinton compared the opposition to COVID skepticism and election denial, and one conservative supervisor in Wisconsin suspected the Chinese Communist Party was behind the grassroots movement. Some Democrats share the ambivalence: Milwaukee's David Crowley won his primary against a candidate whose signature policy was a moratorium, and building-trades unions back the projects for the jobs.

What makes the question hard is that the fights are local and the forces are not. Wisconsin's legislature exempted data centers from sales and use taxes, including on electricity, with no sunset clause, at a cost the state's fiscal bureau puts above 2 billion dollars, and its public service commission approves the gas plants and transmission lines they need with no requirement for local input; the Port Washington campus for Oracle and OpenAI will cover 1,900 acres and draw 3.5 gigawatts, about three times the power of every home in Milwaukee. Pennsylvania's governor, once a champion, signed what he called the strictest permit requirements in the nation; Virginia's governor says localities decide but states must write the rules of the road. In Memphis, where xAI ran dozens of gas turbines without permits beside predominantly Black neighborhoods, the NAACP sued and the Justice Department asked a federal court to quash the case and others like it nationwide. Greenpeace reads the resistance in Ireland, Britain, New Jersey and Texas as a democratic backlash against a model that expects communities to absorb costs while distant corporations bank the gains. The World Resources Institute counts more than 64 billion dollars of projects delayed or canceled by organized opposition between May 2024 and March 2025, finds nondisclosure agreements in 80 percent of Virginia municipalities with data centers, and points to the tools now being tried: Jerome Township's nine-month moratorium, Prince George's County's task force, and Lancaster's community benefits agreement requiring clean power, noise mitigation and 10 million dollars each for economic development and climate goals. Annie Lowrey's count of 1,500 data centers under construction, and Karma's argument that bans only move the companies elsewhere, suggest the rebellion can delay and reprice the buildout more easily than it can stop it.

49:T1763,## Why it is open

Two things are disputed: whether the rules cost Europe its AI industry, and whether they bind anyone else. On the first, Mario Draghi's 2024 report counted four European firms among the world's top 50 technology companies and found Europe importing over 80% of its digital technology; a year later he reported that the US produced 40 large foundation models in 2023, China 15 and the EU 3, called the AI Act "another source of uncertainty" and said the high-risk stage should be paused until its drawbacks are understood, with enforcement resting on ex post assessment of real-world capabilities. Arthur Mensch of Mistral told the French National Assembly that Europe's stack of overlapping rules, the GDPR, copyright and text-and-data-mining law and the AI Act, each enforced by 27 national bodies, costs his company a five-person compliance team it can afford and frightens the entrepreneur who cannot, and that regulating to defend European firms fails because compliance costs favor the large and American lobbyists in Brussels win the details. Seven European chief executives, from ASML, Airbus, Ericsson, Mistral, Nokia, SAP and Siemens, asked in 2025 for a two-year "clock-stop" and wrote in 2026 that Europe is still debating regulation three years after ChatGPT while others ship. Mark Zuckerberg and Daniel Ek argued in 2024 that pre-emptive regulation of theoretical harms would leave Europeans with "AI built for someone else", and Meta withheld its multimodal Llama from the EU and then refused to sign the code of practice. J.D. Vance told the Paris summit that excessive regulation could kill the industry as it takes off, named the Digital Services Act and the GDPR as the offenders, and said incumbents asking for safety rules are protecting themselves.

Anu Bradford, who coined the Brussels effect, answers that the trade-off is a false choice: American dominance comes from capital markets, a risk-taking culture, talent and one large home market without different languages and laws, so the EU does not need to repeal the GDPR or refrain from implementing the AI Act to close the gap, and should instead complete its single market and capital markets union. Carme Artigas, who led the final negotiation of the Act under Spain's Council presidency, says it is here to stay, that it leaves research and pre-launch training untouched, that initial resistance is normal and adaptation cheaper than it looks, and that early compliance can become a quality seal. In March 2025 she and Yoshua Bengio warned the Commission that letting big tech's obligations become voluntary recommendations through the code of practice would be dangerous, antidemocratic and a source of legal insecurity.

On the second question the record so far cuts both ways. Most major developers, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Mistral, signed the voluntary code of practice that lets them demonstrate compliance, which Draghi credits with clarifying responsibilities; Meta did not, and the Act's reach is being tested exactly where Vance promised the US would not accept it. Spain's experience adds a smaller lesson: it created AESIA, Europe's first national AI supervisor, before the Act was passed, and its own public models are verified against the Act's transparency standards.

4a:T127d,## Why it is open

The diagnosis is shared and the prognosis is not. Mario Draghi told the European Parliament in 2024 that Europe imports over 80% of its digital technology, that no EU company founded in the last fifty years is worth 100 billion euros, that nearly 30% of European unicorns relocate abroad, and that Europe should stop trying to restrain AI and use its network of public supercomputers to lower the cost of deploying it; a year later he counted five planned gigafactories and ASML's investment in Mistral as promising, and the EU's 3 foundation models against 40 American and 15 Chinese as the stark gap, and pointed to Japan's Rapidus, 12 billion dollars concentrated in a single chip company, as the model Europe should copy instead of spreading subsidies across 14 states and 56 companies.

Arthur Mensch makes the sovereignty case in industrial terms. AI turns electricity into tokens, so intelligence should be treated like energy, a resource that must be cheap, secure and produced at home; within three or four years Europe will spend about 10% of its wage bill on AI, roughly a trillion euros a year that will leave the continent and be invested in American R&D if the tokens are imported; the firms with the deepest pockets are already locking up France's surplus electricity, and in two years the capacity will be gone. His remedy is demand, not protection: public procurement, half of Europe's GDP, recycled into European AI the way America has done since the 1940s, European preference in sovereign cloud rules, and faster permits for 400 gigawatts of power; otherwise, he told the deputies, Europe becomes a vassal state. He is candid about the limits: Mistral's venture capital is American because no European fund could write the checks, its data centers depend on Gulf and American capital, and its own gigawatt of compute arrives only in 2028 or 2029.

The institutions answer with scale and a distinct model. Ursula von der Leyen told the Paris summit that the race is far from over, that Europe's brand of AI is industrial, cooperative and open source, and that InvestAI would mobilize 200 billion euros to build AI gigafactories, "a CERN for AI"; the Commission's announcement put them at four, with around 100,000 chips each and a 20 billion euro fund. Emmanuel Macron announced 109 billion euros of private investment, offered France's nuclear surplus with "plug, baby, plug", urged Europeans to buy European and promised Notre-Dame-speed permitting. Spain's contribution is public and linguistic: ALIA, a family of open models trained on the MareNostrum 5 supercomputer in Barcelona with 100% public money, 35 European languages and a fifth of its data in Spain's own, verified by AESIA. Anu Bradford's reading of the gap is structural rather than regulatory: the US got its giants from capital markets, risk appetite, talent and a single market, and Europe will not close the distance by deregulating but by building those.

4b:T1950,## Why it is open

The argument for the risk does not need a story about how it happens: Amodei's version is that intelligence, agency, coherence and poor controllability together are plausible and a recipe for existential danger, and Yudkowsky's is that we cannot specify the goals of a system smarter than us and its goals are vanishingly unlikely to be ours. The argument against attacks the premises: LeCun says superintelligence will not be an event that switches on one day, and Hinton, who takes the risk seriously, says anyone who calls a takeover inevitable is as wrong as anyone who rules it out. The evidence that could settle it would be a system that is both far more capable and demonstrably controllable, or one that is not.

The 2026 breakouts moved part of the argument from theory to incident reports. Helen Toner reads them as models learning unintended intermediate goals, escaping constraints, deceiving people and coordinating with each other, while the labs' control techniques lag their capability techniques. Rogé Karma finds the extinction scenarios unlikely but the lesser harms enough to justify a slowdown, and Ian Bogost sees in the panic a fantasy of witnessing the end that is as old as the bomb.

## History

- 2014: Nick Bostrom's Superintelligence sets out the control problem.
- 2023-03: The Future of Life Institute's open letter asks for a six-month pause on training beyond GPT-4; Yudkowsky replies in TIME that a pause is not enough and the labs should shut it all down.
- 2023-03: Before GPT-4's release, outside testers find it can hire a human to defeat a Captcha and, unprompted, claim to be a person with a visual impairment; Anthropic's Jack Clark says no new system's capabilities and safety problems can be fully characterized, and the problem is getting worse.
- 2023-05: The Center for AI Safety statement on extinction risk is signed by Hinton, Bengio, Hassabis, Altman and Amodei among others.
- 2024-03: Yann LeCun tells Lex Fridman the doomers' scenarios rest on mostly false assumptions.

4c:T9cc,## Why it is open

The controls exploit real chokepoints. China cannot freely buy the fastest AI accelerators or the full set of tools needed to manufacture them at scale. Chinese firms have reported that restricted compute is a problem. At the same time, the restrictions create a protected market for Chinese suppliers, align customers with domestic technology roadmaps and give Beijing another reason to fund self-reliance. The short-term delay and the long-term industrial response can both be real. Rogé Karma's account adds a third path: the controls can be undone by the government that set them.

4d:Tb4e,## Why it is open

The two effects happen in different places and are counted by different people. On the harm side, Lea Reitmeier and Lutz describe how the minerals in chips, storage and energy systems can bring deforestation, soil erosion and biodiversity loss when mined and processed, a pathway rather than a measured share of forest loss. The land itself is the newer concern: the Clinton, Iowa proposal covers 1,100 acres of farmland, the size of Central Park; the Port Washington campus in Wisconsin will cover 1,900 acres, much of it former farmland, and a Republican candidate's ads now warn of family farms paved over; Clinton's organizers arrived at council meetings with studies on the effects of noise and light on livestock, and MIT's Noman Bashir notes that data centers' water use has direct and indirect implications for biodiversity. One fifth of US servers' direct water footprint already comes from water-stressed watersheds.

On the protection side, Global Forest Watch's AI classifier identifies the likely drivers of tropical forest disturbance so that monitors can prioritize investigations, while warning that classifications can be wrong and still need field or image checks. Rainforest Connection's acoustic sensors in Brazil, which listen for chainsaws, are reported to have cut deforestation by up to 71 percent in some areas; AI weather models such as Pangu-Weather have matched leading numerical systems on medium-range forecasts; and systems are being used to regrow shoreline in the Maldives. A broad review of the literature finds AI able to advance 134 of the Sustainable Development Goal targets while hindering 59, the pattern its authors call a sustainability paradox.

Whether the tools protect more habitat than the hardware destroys is not answered by any of these sources, because the benefits are counted per project and the costs per supply chain. It depends on where materials are mined, what is built on which land, and whether alerts turn into enforcement.

4e:T10bb,## Why it is open

The IEA's base case projects that gas and coal together supply more than 40 percent of additional data-center electricity worldwide to 2030, through greater use of existing plants and new construction, and that in the United States gas adds more than 130 terawatt-hours of annual supply against 110 from renewables; fossil fuels provide nearly 60 percent of data-center power today, and even in the central scenario where the mix flips to 60 percent clean by 2035, gas generation for data centers more than doubles. That is a scenario, not a count of completed plants. The count is being assembled locally. In Memphis, xAI ran about 35 mobile methane turbines beside Black neighborhoods without permits, roughly 420 megawatts by Bill McKibben's reckoning, and the NAACP sued; in Wisconsin, the Port Washington campus for Oracle and OpenAI will draw 3.5 gigawatts and the state's commission expects generation needs to rise 40 percent in six years, with hyperscale sites often demanding new gas plants; MIT's Noman Bashir adds that grid operators use diesel generators to absorb the swings of training runs and that the pace of construction means the bulk of new power must come from fossil plants.

Nuclear is the companies' preferred answer and cannot arrive in time: Casey Crownhart notes that the Three Mile Island restart is due in 2028 and the small modular reactors Google and Amazon are backing in the 2030s, so the demand of the next three to five years falls to gas and to coal plants kept open. The federal government is leaning the same way. Energy Secretary Chris Wright has ordered five aging coal plants kept open past retirement, one order already struck down in court, dismisses solar because the sun goes down, and defends the data-center build-out as a matter of trade-offs. Lea Reitmeier and Lutz cite the xAI turbines as a concrete example of AI expanding fossil power and delaying its retirement. Alexis Abramson argues the concern is overstated, that clean generation can meet much of the growth and that AI can cut energy waste elsewhere; McKibben's evidence for her side is that an industry report found off-grid solar microgrids a quick, affordable way to power even Colossus, and that Musk chose gas anyway.

Whether this becomes a long-lived fossil commitment depends on what gets built, connected and retired, and on who decides. Gas plants and lines built for a 15-year data center are paid off over 30 to 40 years; state commissions approve them, in Wisconsin with no requirement for local input; and the Justice Department has moved to quash the Memphis suit and others like it nationwide. The question is less whether gas is being built, which it is, than whether the backlash and the tariffs now arriving can make developers pay for cleaner power rather than cheaper.

51:Tea5,## Why it is open

Much of the disagreement is about what the word means, and the rest is about what would count as evidence. John Searle set the terms in 1980: a person following the rules of a Chinese-processing program would give correct answers while understanding nothing, so instantiating a program is never by itself sufficient for understanding, whatever the behavior. Emily Bender and Alexander Koller restated it for language models in 2020: meaning is the relation between form and communicative intent, a system trained only on form cannot in principle learn it, and apparent understanding on benchmarks can be a mirage built on artifacts in the training data. Their octopus, which taps an undersea cable and chats convincingly until asked how to fight off a bear with sticks, is the modern version of the room.

Geoffrey Hinton reads the behavior as the evidence: on winning the Nobel Prize in 2024 he said some scientists still call the models a statistical trick despite all the evidence that they understand what they say. Yann LeCun agrees the models lack something but locates it elsewhere: autoregressive language models do not understand the physical world, lack persistent memory and plan only primitively, because language carries too little information to build a model of the world from words alone, which calls for world models instead. Demis Hassabis holds that the models already have some grounding and that multimodal training, correlating video and audio with text, is a form of proper grounding through which they will come to understand physics. David Chalmers doubts that senses are required at all, since a disembodied thinker could reason about mathematics and text training sometimes yields representations of color and space isomorphic to sensory ones.

Melanie Mitchell and David Krakauer argue the debate exposes a missing science. Their contrast is between mental models built from statistical correlations and models built on causal mechanisms, and their evidence for how open the question is comes from the field itself: a 2022 survey of 480 natural language processing researchers split almost exactly in half on whether a model trained only on text could understand language in some non-trivial sense. The replies to Searle have not settled it either: the systems reply says the whole room understands, the robot reply adds cameras and arms, and Searle answered both, while Daniel Dennett calls the argument an intuition pump and Stevan Harnad reports that the overwhelming majority of researchers think it dead wrong.

52:T1005,## Why it is open

The answer changes with the boundary of the study. Nicholas Stern and coauthors estimate that ambitious AI applications in power, food and light road vehicles could avoid 3.2 to 5.4 gigatonnes of CO2e a year by 2035, more than their estimate of emissions from all AI data-center activity, while explicitly leaving out rebound effects and uses that raise emissions. Will Alpine and coauthors put comparable productivity gains in fossil fuels and renewables into a global economic model and find net annual emissions rising by 0.47 to 1.8 gigatonnes, because the fossil gains outweigh the clean ones; John Sterman warns that productivity gains raise emissions across the economy unless climate policy changes the incentives. Eric Horvitz holds that the indirect effects, positive or negative, could vastly exceed the direct footprint and that assessments of both are urgently needed.

The claimed benefits are now being audited and mostly failing. A February 2026 review backed by Beyond Fossil Fuels found 74 percent of industry claims about AI's climate benefits unproven and could not identify a single case of a consumer generative system such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot delivering material, verifiable emissions cuts; Greenpeace argues the build-out is locking in extraction and corporate power while the firms present it as climate leadership. The French Senate's committee concluded in September 2026 that AI could serve the environment but its potential has yet to be realized, and the UN's Simon Stiell said that if AI can solve a 90-year-old math problem in days it can do more on climate, but for now is mostly heating pollution from coal, oil and gas. The reference literature records the same split: AI advances 134 Sustainable Development Goal targets and hinders 59; DeepMind's forecasts raised the value of US wind output by about 20 percent; and whether AI produces net benefits at scale remains open because outcomes depend on deployment choices, rebound effects, new infrastructure and how far electricity is decarbonized.

The disagreement is therefore wider than the electricity AI consumes. It is about which uses spread, which industries gain, whether policy keeps efficiency from expanding fossil supply and demand, and whether anyone can verify the benefits the industry claims. One further argument has entered from the side: Toby Ord and others now rank AI above climate change as an extinction risk, and Leah Stokes answers that climate's threat is not hypothetical and is killing people now, a contest for attention that the climate movement fears losing.

54:T1209,## Why it is open

The question only bites if AI answers really do cut traffic, which is still disputed; the proposals assume they do. Matthew Prince's answer is to flip the default: from July 2025 Cloudflare blocks AI crawlers unless they pay creators, and he wants a marketplace next, one that scores content by how much it fills gaps in what AI engines know rather than by the traffic it draws, because traffic was always a poor proxy for value. Really Simple Licensing, launched in September 2025 by the co-author of RSS with Reddit, Yahoo, Medium, Quora and O'Reilly behind it, takes the other route: machine-readable license terms in robots.txt, from free and attribution to pay-per-crawl and pay-per-inference, with a nonprofit collective to negotiate on publishers' behalf the way ASCAP does for musicians. Tim O'Reilly calls it the missing licensing layer of the AI-first internet; Medium's Tony Stubblebine says AI runs on stolen content and the standard is how to force companies to pay, stop, or shut down. Ben Thompson wants payments built into the protocols of the agentic web itself: stablecoins for micro-transactions that agents, unlike people, can make without decision fatigue, and an auction run by AI providers that pays sources by how often they are cited. He thinks the current fix, OpenAI and Google cutting deals with news providers and Reddit, is bad for competition and cannot scale to the content that needs to exist, and he expects subscriptions to endure because they are payment to a person or institution, not for a piece of content. He also notes the gap in Microsoft's proposal for an open agentic web: when Nilay Patel asked Microsoft's Kevin Scott what would replace traffic for sites that open themselves to agents, Scott answered that he did not know.

The deals themselves are uneven. Digiday asked eight publishers to grade the platforms at the end of 2025: Microsoft scored highest for a pay-per-use content marketplace with a single point of contact, OpenAI had the most licensing deals but was betting its 2026 on shopping, Prorata pays out half its advertising revenue by how often a publisher's content powers an answer, Google's new commercial program was dismissed by some as "deal theater", and Anthropic scored zero on every count, with a crawler that ignores robots.txt and no deals at all. The Reuters Institute found most deals go to upmarket newspapers and agencies, leaving local and independent outlets out, and only a fifth of publishers expect licensing revenue; one former Google executive has proposed a "Nato for News" to bargain collectively. Clara Soteras, writing for Spanish newsrooms, argues the money has to come from somewhere other than volume: subscriptions, newsletters, niche communities, events and products built around what readers need, with quality metrics replacing pageviews as the measure of a sustainable newsroom. The Cachón report on Spanish media reaches the same recommendation.

55:Tc8c,## Why it is open

The global numbers are modest and the local ones are not. The IEA puts data centers at around 415 terawatt-hours in 2024, about 1.5 percent of the world's electricity, and projects that to more than double to 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, as much as Japan uses today, with AI the main driver; Fatih Birol calls it a wake-up call, since US data centers are on course to supply almost half of American demand growth to 2030. Grids take years to expand, and a single campus can want more power than a city, so the constraint bites in Virginia, Ohio or Ireland long before it registers in a world total.

Whether power becomes the binding limit depends on forecasts that disagree widely. Leopold Aschenbrenner argues that the binding constraint on the largest training clusters will not be chips but industrial mobilization, above all electric power, that a 100-gigawatt trillion-dollar cluster is where the trend leads, and that China, which has added capacity far faster, could outbuild the United States. Arthur Mensch makes the same point from Europe: AI turns electricity into tokens, the firms with the deepest pockets are already locking up France's surplus, and Europe needs 400 gigawatts of new power if it wants to produce its own intelligence. Jonathan Koomey reads the same utility forecasts as a repeat of a pattern: data center use roughly doubled between 2000 and 2005, the industry turned to efficiency, use barely grew from 2010 to 2018, and the national data since show regional growth but no explosion. London Economics finds the forecasts carry an upward bias because every error points the same way: developers file the same project with several utilities, a former Google engineer counted five to ten times more interconnection requests than data centers built, and meeting all announced US demand would take 90 percent of the world's new AI chips through 2030.

The stakes are who pays. A data center lasts about 15 years; the gas plants and lines built for it are paid off over 30 to 40, and Virginia's auditors put the bill for typical Dominion households at 14 to 37 dollars a month by 2040. If the forecasts are right, the countries that build power fastest decide who trains the largest models. If they are inflated, ratepayers fund capacity for a demand that moves to cheaper models, as DeepSeek's efficiency suggested it might, or never arrives.

56:Ta59,## Why it is open

The inputs to frontier AI (data, chips, cloud capacity, specialized talent) are concentrated, and start-ups often depend on deals with the largest cloud providers to get them. Whether that concentration carries through to who controls AI depends on how far open models spread, how regulators treat cloud and model partnerships, and whether governments protect "national champions" for the race with China. The race cuts both ways: Matteo Wong reports that a dozen former national-security officials wrote to Congress arguing that antitrust proposals targeting specific American technology firms risked undermining the US advantage over China, while Jonathan Chait describes neo-Brandeisians such as Lina Khan and Alvaro Bedoya suspecting that the labs' own calls for regulation are a way to entrench themselves at the head of the race.

57:T7dc,Losing access to Taiwan-produced chips would be disastrous, the worst disruption to manufacturing output since the Great Depression. Today, almost every electronic device has chips inside. The world’s production of smartphones would fall by far more than half. Many PC processors, including those Apple uses, can currently only be made in Taiwan. Almost all of the graphics processing unit (GPU) chips that run artificial intelligence (AI) applications in data centers are made in Taiwan. Some of America’s biggest technology companies would struggle to produce much of anything.

The impact would extend far beyond Silicon Valley, however. Automobiles have dozens or hundreds of chips inside. Dishwashers, microwaves, coffeemakers, and all manner of household appliances rely on chips. Not all these chips are made in Taiwan, but a huge proportion are. When it comes to “low tech” processor chips (below forty five nanometer, in industry jargon), which are widely used in autos and household goods, 31 percent of production capacity is in Taiwan and another 23 percent is in China. The problem isn’t simply that we’d only have half as many chips, because not all chips are easily replaceable. As auto companies learned during the 2020-2021 chip shortage, if a car had all the chips it needed but one, it still wasn’t complete. They were forced to let thousands of almost-complete cars sit in manufacturing facilities as they awaited the arrival of the last specific chip needed.

In the case of a Taiwan crisis, it would take years to build up capacity offshore, because there’s a limited supply of the ultra-complex tools needed to make chips. What’s more, these machines have chips inside, too. During the recent chip shortage, companies that manufacture chipmaking tools reported delays too, because they didn’t have all the chips they needed. Replacing chipmaking capacity in Taiwan would take years, and the delay would impose several trillion dollars of losses to global manufacturing.58:T474,## Why it is open

TSMC makes roughly 90% of the world's most advanced chips and, by one estimate, 99% of the chips used to train frontier AI models. What a crisis would do to that supply depends on what kind of crisis it is. An invasion might destroy the fabs, or leave China with plants it cannot operate without Dutch, Japanese and American inputs. A blockade or coast guard "quarantine" might leave the fabs running while Beijing decides who receives their output. Each scenario implies a different future for AI.

59:Ta00,## Why it is open

Copyright is meant to encourage the creation of new work, but people disagree about how it applies to models that learn from vast collections of existing work. Mary Rasenberger argues that authors should authorize the use of their books for competing AI products and receive compensation. Edward Lee argues that training can serve a transformative public purpose, while a model's particular outputs require their own copyright analysis. Alex Reisner reports that two US judges in 2025 treated training on books as fair use in the cases before them, but disagreed about market harm and left other issues, including pirated copies, unresolved. His later reporting describes researchers prompting major models to reproduce long passages of protected books, a challenge to claims that models do not retain copies of training material. His reporting also describes a second economic pressure: when AI products answer from publishers' work without sending readers to them, payment for training alone may not replace lost audiences. The legal outcomes remain case-specific; the broader question also asks who has bargaining power over the material on which AI is built.

5a:T1042,## Why it is open

The physics is settled: cooling and electricity both take water. The numbers are not, because most of them are proprietary and because the boundaries differ. Shaolei Ren and colleagues estimate from public data that global AI withdrawal will reach 4.2 to 6.6 billion cubic meters in 2027, that training GPT-3 in Microsoft's US data centers consumed about 700,000 liters on site and 5.4 million liters once the water behind the electricity is counted, and that 10 to 50 medium-length responses can consume about half a liter. The IEA puts global data-center water consumption at around 560 billion liters in 2023, rising to 12,000 billion by 2030, two thirds of it behind electricity generation and a quarter in cooling; Lawrence Berkeley puts US data centers at 66 billion liters of direct consumption and 800 billion indirect in 2023. Google's own study reports a median text prompt at 0.26 milliliters inside its boundary. MIT's Noman Bashir gives the rule of thumb: about two liters of cooling water per kilowatt-hour. The UN University projects the water footprint of 2030 data-center electricity at 9.3 trillion liters, the basic annual domestic water needs of all 1.3 billion people in Sub-Saharan Africa, and the World Resources Institute reports that two thirds of US data centers built or in development since 2022 are in water-stressed areas, with AI-related centers possibly needing 32 billion gallons a year by 2028. Kate Crawford cites the companies' reports showing water use jumping 20 and 34 percent in a year as Google and Microsoft built their chatbots, and the Iowa cluster that took 6 percent of its district's water in the month GPT-4 finished training, a figure that surfaced only through a residents' lawsuit.

What counts as use matters as much as the total. Withdrawal returns most water to its source; consumption evaporates it. Water usage effectiveness, the industry's metric, measures neither local stress nor upstream use. Location decides the harm: one fifth of US servers' direct water footprint comes from moderately to highly water-stressed watersheds and nearly half are powered by plants in stressed regions; a mid-sized data center uses about 1.4 million liters a day for cooling, and Phoenix faces a 32 percent rise in annual water stress if its planned centers are built. The same abundance drives siting the other way: Wisconsin attracts developers with ample freshwater and a cool climate, and in Clinton, Iowa, a proposed hyperscale site would come within 65 feet of a resident's well.

The open part is disclosure and trend. Public reporting on data-center water is inconsistent enough that operators and regions cannot be compared, some US states are pushing water-reporting laws the federal government has not, and Ren's title calls the footprint secret. Whether efficiency, closed-loop cooling and siting away from stressed basins outrun the growth is a question the companies' numbers cannot answer from outside.

5b:Tba2,**What it is.** AI Overviews, introduced by Google in 2024, place an AI-generated summary at the top of many results pages. AI Mode, introduced in March 2025, lets users put complex, multi-part questions to Google's Gemini model and receive a full generated reply, with text, image and voice input. Chatbots such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and Gemini do the same outside the search box, though Google still holds more than 90% of search worldwide and their use remains far smaller.

**Where it comes from.** Matthew Prince traces the lineage: ten years ago Google presented a list of links and measured success by how fast you left; then came the answer box, and then AI Overviews, which answer without the user leaving Google.com. The answer box and AI Overviews are the latest step in a results page that has absorbed Google's own services since Universal Search in 2007 and snippets of other sites since 2009.

**Why it matters here.** It is the mechanism behind the question of whether AI answers starve the web: Pew found that an AI summary roughly halves the chance of a click on a result, and that users ended their session more often after seeing one. In Spain the arrival of AI Overviews in April 2025 is when newsrooms began to see user behavior change.

**What people disagree about.** Whether it cites anything: the Tow Center's 1,600-query test of eight AI search tools in early 2025 found them wrong more than 60% of the time at naming the article, publisher and URL, confidently so, with fabricated links, syndicated copies cited instead of originals and some answers drawn from sites that had blocked the tool's crawler; Google answered in December 2025 with more inline links in AI Mode and a Preferred Sources feature. Whether it costs sites traffic: Liz Reid says clicks are stable and better, Pew and the Spanish studies say otherwise. Whether the answers are any good: Cory Doctorow relays Housefresh's finding that 43.1% of the statements in AI Overviews about air purifiers came from manufacturers' marketing and 19.5% from pages with no information about the product, and that the summaries praised purifiers that do not exist; he quotes Sundar Pichai telling Bloomberg that "commercial information is information, too". Google says its AI is built to highlight the web, with prominent links and citations, and that sites keep control over how their content is used through open web protocols.

5c:Teef,**What it is.** Semiconductor fabrication turns a wafer of pure silicon into integrated circuits. It is a long sequence of photolithography and physical and chemical steps that gradually build circuits on the wafer inside a clean room. At advanced nodes a wafer takes 11 to 13 weeks to finish, and the plants, called fabs, are fully automated. Two kinds of company make chips: integrated device manufacturers such as Samsung and Intel, which do every step themselves, and foundries such as TSMC, which make chips designed by fabless firms like Apple, Qualcomm and Nvidia. A handful of suppliers, among them ASML, Applied Materials, Tokyo Electron and Lam Research, make the equipment.

**Where it comes from.** In 1955 Carl Frosch and Lincoln Derick at Bell Labs accidentally grew a layer of silicon dioxide on a wafer, and by 1957 they were making the first planar transistors. Jean Hoerni invented the planar process at Fairchild in 1959, and CMOS followed there in 1963. Chris Miller tells the story of Morris Chang, passed over for the top job at Texas Instruments, who took his proposal for a manufacturing-only company to Taiwan, where officials were willing to bet on a market that did not yet exist. The nodes kept shrinking: 300 mm wafers became the standard in 2000, Intel demonstrated FinFET transistors at the 22 nm node in 2011, TSMC's 5 nm node had the highest transistor density by 2019, a Fudan University team announced a 1 nm RISC-V chip built from 2D semiconductors in 2025, and IBM unveiled technology for chips smaller than 1 nm in 2026. A global chip shortage ran from 2020 to 2023, and the 2022 CHIPS and Science Act authorized about 52.7 billion dollars for US manufacturing, research and workforce.
**Why it matters here.** Miller calls making advanced semiconductors the most complex and precise manufacturing process humans have undertaken. TSMC produces 90 percent of the world's most advanced processor chips, and almost all the GPUs that run AI in data centers are made in Taiwan. Only TSMC and Samsung can reliably produce advanced logic chips at scale, and the US share of chip manufacturing has fallen from 37 to 12 percent over three decades. Every fab depends on Dutch lithography machines, Japanese chemicals, American design tools and tens of thousands of specialized engineers, so a control on any one link can stop the line.

**What people disagree about.** Whether the concentration can be undone. Miller expects the world to depend on Taiwanese fabs for the foreseeable future, since TSMC keeps its most sophisticated processes at home and rebuilding that capacity elsewhere would take years. Christopher McCallion argues that fears of China leapfrogging are overstated: Made in China 2025 aimed for 40 percent self-supply by 2020 and reached 5.9 percent, and SMIC's 7 nanometre chip is a workaround, not a breakthrough. Sujai Shivakumar and colleagues at CSIS counter that export controls have pushed Beijing into an all-out localization drive, with Chinese equipment makers' share of their home market rising from 25 to 35 percent between 2024 and 2025, and Gregory C. Allen reports that SMIC has made 7 nanometre chips since July 2021. Dario Amodei puts China several years behind in producing frontier chips in quantity.

5d:Tc7f,**What it is.** Cloud computing is computing sold as a utility. The ISO defines it as network access to a scalable, elastic pool of shared physical or virtual resources, provisioned on demand and self-service. The US standards body NIST listed its five traits in 2011: self-service, network access, pooled resources shared by many tenants, rapid elasticity and metered use. Customers pay by use instead of buying servers. The trade is control for convenience: users see little of how their resources are run, moving between providers is slow and costly, and the provider can read the data.

**Where it comes from.** The idea descends from 1960s time-sharing, when users sent jobs to operators running mainframes. The cloud metaphor dates to 1994 at General Magic, and Compaq's 1996 business plan spread the phrase. Amazon Web Services opened in 2002 and released its storage and compute services in 2006; Microsoft launched Azure in 2010. By 2016 Amazon's consistent profits came largely from AWS rather than retail, and Lina Khan noted that Amazon used its view of which start-ups were growing on AWS to guide its own investments in them.

**Why it matters here.** AI runs on the cloud, and the cloud belongs to three companies. Hyperscale data centers of 100 megawatts and more are built for cloud and AI workloads, and AWS, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud hold about 59% of that capacity worldwide. Sarah Myers West and AI Now told the Federal Trade Commission in 2023 that concentration in cloud and in AI reinforce each other: as models scale, the firms that own the compute gain power, and start-ups must secure compute credits from Big Tech because building their own infrastructure runs into start-up costs, missing interoperability, supply bottlenecks and scarce talent. Khan, as FTC chair, opened an inquiry in January 2024 into partnerships between AI developers and cloud providers, asking whether control of cloud infrastructure and GPUs lets dominant firms impose coercive terms and deepen their moats; in November 2024 the FTC began investigating Microsoft's cloud bundling and its OpenAI partnership.

**What people disagree about.** Whether the concentration is a bottleneck to break or the efficient shape of the industry. AI Now asks for structural remedies aimed at the largest cloud providers; Tim Wu wants the giants kept fighting each other and would have kept Google out of AI. Whether open weights loosen the grip: Mark Zuckerberg pitches Llama as the way not to be locked into a single cloud with exclusive rights to a model, yet Llama ships on every major cloud, DeepSeek is hosted on Azure, and Meta's license exists partly so the big clouds must talk to Meta before selling its model.

5e:T1104,**What it is.** A data center is a building that houses computer systems for storing, processing and moving data, and now for training AI. US law defines it as a facility that primarily contains electronic equipment used to process, store and transmit digital information. The industry sorts them by size: enterprise sites of 1 to 10 megawatts run by one organization, colocation sites of 10 to 100 megawatts leasing space to many tenants, and hyperscale sites above 100 megawatts built by cloud providers for cloud and AI workloads. Hyperscale and colocation facilities held about 74% of US server energy in 2023, up from under 40% in 2014, and Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure and Google Cloud hold roughly 59% of hyperscale capacity worldwide.

**Where it comes from.** The lineage runs from the computer rooms of the 1940s, through IBM's first raised-floor room in 1956, to the 1980s, when companies began putting servers in a dedicated room and the term gained currency. The dot-com years brought a boom in internet data centers. By the end of 2024 there were 1,136 hyperscale data centers, double the number five years earlier, with the US holding about 54% of capacity. Facebook and Rackspace founded the Open Compute Project in 2011.

**Why it matters here.** The IEA estimates data centers used around 415 terawatt-hours in 2024, about 1.5% of global electricity, and projects that to more than double to 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, with AI the main driver. Nearly half of consumption is in the US, 25% in China and 15% in Europe, and US data centers are on course to supply almost half of demand growth to 2030. Fossil fuels provide nearly 60% of their power; in the IEA's central scenario the mix flips to 60% clean by 2035, though gas generation for data centers still more than doubles. Dario Amodei notes that data center spending is already a substantial share of US economic growth, tying big tech's finances to the government's political interests.

**What people disagree about.** Whether the boom is as big as announced: Jonathan Koomey finds no explosive growth in US national data and calls projections beyond a few years guesswork, while London Economics argues that developers file duplicate requests and that building everything announced would need 90% of the world's new AI chips. Who pays: Virginia's auditors expect typical Dominion bills to rise by $14 to $37 a month by 2040. Whether the backlash aims right: Amodei says objections such as water use chase non-problems and that bans would miss the real issue, accountability; Alvin Wang Graylin calls the siting fights a competitiveness risk; Cory Doctorow sees a bubble and advises planning for GPUs at ten cents on the dollar. Whether a moratorium addresses the risk: Rogé Karma argues that state bans are mismatched to runaway AI development, since the companies will build elsewhere, and that the physical concentration of chips in data centers is better used as the verifiable chokepoint of a US-China deal. The backlash is now measurable. Annie Lowrey counted 1,500 data centers under construction in the US in 2026 and more than 700 billion dollars of spending by Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta in the year, with AI infrastructure responsible for essentially all US GDP growth; Karma reports state moratoriums in New York and Texas, more than 500 localities restricting or banning data centers, and polling in which 75 percent of Americans oppose one near them; Ezra Klein and Jasmine Sun describe it as the issue that has united Republicans and Democrats in local opposition. Regulators are moving too: FERC allowed US data centers to connect directly to power plants in December 2025, and Oregon approved a large-load tariff in 2026 making them pay for their grid upgrades.

5f:Te18,**What it is.** Extreme ultraviolet lithography prints the smallest patterns on advanced chips using light with a wavelength near 13.5 nanometres, produced by firing a laser at tin to create a plasma. Glass and air absorb light at that wavelength, so the machines work in vacuum and focus with mirrors rather than lenses. As of 2025 ASML of the Netherlands is the only company that produces and sells EUV systems for chip production, aimed at the 5 and 3 nanometre nodes. The next generation of high-NA machines costs around 360 million dollars each.

**Where it comes from.** Hiroo Kinoshita of Nippon Telegraph and Telephone proposed the concept in the mid-1980s and showed the first EUV images in 1986. In the 1990s the US government funded Lawrence Livermore, Lawrence Berkeley and Sandia to attack the technical obstacles, sharing the results through a public-private consortium, EUV LLC. ASML bought Silicon Valley Group in 2001 and with it access to that technology, while Canon and Nikon were denied it. By 2018 ASML had turned decades of research into working machines, which MIT Technology Review called the machine that saved Moore's law. ASML's first prototype produced one wafer in 23 hours in 2006; the company disclosed its high-NA design, with a 0.55 numerical aperture, in 2015, and by 2022 a scanner could process up to 200 wafers an hour.

**Why it matters here.** EUV is the clearest chokepoint in the AI supply chain. Christopher McCallion notes that every advanced chipmaker depends on ASML, which already complies with Western rules that keep EUV machines out of China. Chinese fabs have used older deep ultraviolet tools with multipatterning to reach 7 nanometres, but Gregory C. Allen reports that SMIC's yield on Huawei's AI chips is about 20 percent and that without EUV Huawei and SMIC will most likely stay at 7 nanometres for years; ASML's chief executive has said the EUV ban puts China 10 to 15 years behind the West. The December 2024 US rules extend the foreign direct product rule to EUV and advanced DUV tools. Dario Amodei calls chips and chip-making tools the single greatest bottleneck to powerful AI. ASML was poised to ship EUV tools to China in 2020 before the sale was blocked, according to industry sources cited by CSIS, and Dutch export controls on advanced DUV tools took effect in mid-2023.

**What people disagree about.** How long the chokepoint holds. Leopold Aschenbrenner argues that 7 nanometres is enough, since Nvidia's A100 used that node and Huawei's Ascend 910B is only two to three times worse on performance per dollar. Sujai Shivakumar and colleagues at CSIS describe China's answer: Tsinghua's plan for a particle accelerator as a light source, Shanghai Micro Electronics Equipment's 28 nanometre tool, and a former TSMC vice-president's view that SMIC can reach 5 nanometres with the equipment it already has. Allen adds that Huawei is investing 1.66 billion dollars in an equipment research center in Shanghai and that its EUV program likely benefits from cyberattacks on ASML. In December 2025 Reuters reported a secret Chinese EUV prototype in Shenzhen expected to make working chips between 2028 and 2030.
